leads.title: bounty: implement deterministic LLM behavioral guardrails and policy enforcement engine for automated responses
leads.description:
### 📋 Problem Statement
The automated response generator (`backend/services/gemini_service.py`) returns raw LLM output directly to end-users without deterministic guardrail validation. This presents serious enterprise risks: prompt injection attacks, unauthorized commitments (e.g. AI promising refunds or SLA guarantees exceeding company policy), leaking internal infrastructure URLs, or failing to redact confidential PII. We require a robust, deterministic guardrail pipeline (inspired by Parlant / NeMo Guardrails) that enforces organizational policy constraints before any message is sent.

### ✅ Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Create `PolicyGuardrailEngine` in `backend/services/rule_engine.py` with deterministic validation rules (e.g., forbidden commitment keywords, max credit limits, URL whitelisting).
- [ ] Intercept LLM generated drafts before persistence/delivery; validate output against defined company policy schemas.
- [ ] If confidence is below threshold (<0.85) or a policy constraint is violated, automatically block auto-resolution, tag ticket for human escalation (`status: "pending_human"`), and log the policy violation in `audit_logs`.
- [ ] Run cryptographic PII redaction pass on the output ensuring no sensitive numbers/tokens appear in plain text.
- [ ] Add comprehensive test suite in `backend/tests/test_policy_guardrails.py` covering prompt injection detection, policy boundary enforcement, and human escalation triggers.

### 📂 Relevant File Paths
- `backend/services/gemini_service.py`
- `backend/services/rule_engine.py`
- `backend/services/pii_redactor.py`
- `backend/routers/ai.py`
- `backend/tests/test_policy_guardrails.py`

### 🧪 Testing Instructions
Run pytest on policy guardrails test suite:
```bash
pytest backend/tests/test_policy_guardrails.py -v
```

---
This issue is part of GSSoC 2026. Please read the [Contributor Onboarding Guide](https://github.com/riteshbonthalakoti/HELPDESK.AI/blob/gssoc/docs/GSSoC_DEV_ONBOARDING.md) before starting.

leads.title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy. Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist. ApiClay makes that whole loop easier. You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live. But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace. If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links. You can also turn what you already have into an API: * MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints. * Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API. * Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing. * Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products. For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data. There are also practical data tools beyond discovery: * Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result. * Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes. * Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs. * Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper. For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use. *ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.* We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: Python API primes_up_to(0) IndexError and primes_up_to(-5) returns wrong primes; sliding_window(_,0) returns empty windows
leads.description:
### Lateralus version

lateralus-lang 3.2.0

### Python version

Python 3.13.7

### Operating System

Linux

### Component

Standard Library

### Bug description

Two edge-case bugs in the Python API of lateralus_lang.algorithms
(the .ltl stdlib version already guards n < 2, so this is a
Python-port-only correctness/isolation issue):

1) primes_up_to(0)  -> IndexError: list assignment index out of range
   primes_up_to(-5) -> [2, 3]  (bogus; negative ranges produce primes)

2) sliding_window([1,2,3], 0) -> [[], [], [], []]
   Silent semantic trap: no error, plausible-looking output.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
// NOTE: this edge case is only reachable through the Python API
// (the .ltl stdlib primes_up_to already guards `n < 2`).
// Minimal Python reproducer is in "Actual behavior" below.
import algorithms

fn main() {
    print(primes_up_to(10))   // [2, 3, 5, 7] — correct
}
```

### Expected behavior

primes_up_to(0)             -> []
primes_up_to(-5)            -> []
sliding_window([1,2,3], 0)  -> Value error (or [])

### Actual behavior

```shell
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to, sliding_window"
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to; primes_up_to(0)"
IndexError: list assignment index out of range
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to; print(primes_up_to(-5))"
[2, 3]
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import sliding_window; print(sliding_window([1,2,3], 0))"
[[], [], [], []]
```

### Additional context

Suggested fix:
    def primes_up_to(n: int) -> list:
        if n < 2:
            return []
        ...
    def sliding_window(arr: list, size: int) -> list:
        if size <= 0:
            raise ValueError("window size must be a positive integer")
        ...

Drafted with AI assistance; all four commands above were executed on
lateralus-lang 3.2.0 / Python 3.13.7 / Linux and pasted verbatim.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: chunk(arr, 0) infinite-loops in .ltl stdlib; Python API raises raw ValueError
leads.description:
### Lateralus version

lateralus-lang 3.2.0

### Python version

Python 3.13.7

### Operating System

Linux

### Component

Standard Library

### Bug description

algorithms.chunk(arr, 0) has no size validation. In the .ltl stdlib version it
hangs forever (while-loop never advances because i = i + size with size == 0),
which freezes the VM with no error and no way to Ctrl+C from inside generated
code. In the Python API it raises a raw `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be
zero`, which is an implementation detail leaking to the user.

Expected: a clear, early Value error for size <= 0 in both implementations.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
import algorithms

fn main() {
    print("before")
    print(chunk([1, 2, 3], 0))   // hangs forever (never reaches "after")
    print("after")
}
```

### Expected behavior

Error before any work: chunk size must be a positive integer
(the program should exit non-zero, not hang)

### Actual behavior

```shell
# .ltl stdlib path — hangs forever (no error, CPU 100%, Ctrl+C needed)
$ lateralus run chunk_zero.ltl
before
^C

# Python API path:
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import chunk; chunk([1,2,3], 0)"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lateralus_lang/algorithms.py", line 129, in chunk
    return [lst[i:i+n] for i in range(0, len(lst), n)]
ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero
```

### Additional context

Root cause (.ltl stdlib/algorithms.ltl):
    while i < len(arr) {
        let end = min(i + size, len(arr))
        result = result + [slice(arr, i, end)]
        i = i + size          # size == 0 → i never advances → infinite loop
    }
Suggested fix: guard size <= 0 (raise or return []) before the loop.

Python port (lateralus_lang/algorithms.py):
    def chunk(arr, size):
        return [arr[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(arr), size)]
Suggested fix:
    if size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("chunk size must be a positive integer")

Environment: lateralus-lang 3.2.0 (PyPI), Python 3.13.7, Linux x86_64.
Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed before posting.

At that point, workflow automation basically did not work. The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish. Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth. So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents. The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer. You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need. For example, we might already know: * Address that you already have in the CRM * Company description from the internet * What a agreement document must contain * How a good answer should be Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”. The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later. On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue. Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here. I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case. My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today? If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/ Docs: https://docs.formstep.io I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

leads.title: [bounty]: bug-report: Python optional pipeline silently converts valid falsy results to nil
leads.description:
### Lateralus version

3.2.0 (from pyproject.toml and lateralus_lang.__version__; tested commit d078809df3f5db544b7efa7b0979c7a43ebb25e6)

### Python version

Python 3.11.9

### Operating System

Windows

### Component

Compiler / Parser

### Bug description

The Python backend incorrectly converts valid falsy return values into `None` (`nil`) when using the optional pipeline operator `|?`.

When the input is not `nil`, the operator should call the function and preserve its return value. However, the generated Python code uses the `and ... or None` pattern, which incorrectly replaces falsy results such as `0`, `false`, `""`, `[]`, and `0.0` with `None`.

**Minimal example:**

```text
import io
fn zero(x: int) -> int { return 0 }
let result = 5 |? zero
io.println(result)
```

**Expected result:** `0`

**Actual result:** `None`

**Generated Python code:**

```python
result = ((_opt_val := 5) is not None and zero(_opt_val) or None)
```

The issue affects both direct function references and function calls with additional arguments.

The bug was reproduced in 10 test cases, with 5 additional control tests passing.

**Affected file:** `lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py`, lines 1492–1502.

**Tested version:** Lateralus 3.2.0, commit `d078809df3f5db544b7efa7b0979c7a43ebb25e6`.

This is a correctness bug that can silently cause data loss in optional pipelines.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
import io

fn zero(x: int) -> int {
    return 0
}

let result = 5 |? zero
io.println(result)
```

### Expected behavior

The optional pipeline operator `|?` should execute the function when the input is not `nil` and preserve its return value.

In this example, the function `zero(5)` returns `0`, so the expected output is:

```
0
```

Valid falsy values such as `0`, `false`, `""`, `[]`, and `0.0` must not be converted to `None`.

### Actual behavior

```shell
The program compiles successfully but prints `None` instead of `0`.

The Python backend generates:


result = ((_opt_val := 5) is not None and zero(_opt_val) or None)


Because `zero(_opt_val)` returns `0`, the Python `or None` expression incorrectly replaces the valid result with `None`.

This causes silent loss of valid falsy values.
```

### Additional context

**Additional testing evidence:**

- Tested on Lateralus 3.2.0 (Python backend).
- 15 regression tests executed in an isolated Windows AppContainer.
- 10 test cases reproduced the bug.
- 5 control tests passed.
- No matching duplicate was found among the inspected public issues, pull requests, and comments at the time of testing.

**Bounty eligibility:**

I would like to submit this report for the recurring $10 bug-report micro-bounty described in BOUNTIES.md.

The investigation was completed before opening a reservation issue. I understand this differs from the project's pre-claim procedure.

Could the maintainer please confirm whether this report is still eligible for the bounty?

I can provide the full regression results and additional reproduction

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: Python-keyword identifiers emitted unchanged — `let from = 1` generates invalid Python
leads.description:
The Python code-generator emits `Ident` nodes as bare `node.name` with no escaping (codegen/python.py line ~1468). If a Lateralus identifier collides with a Python keyword the generated source is a `SyntaxError`.

**Minimal reproducer:**

```
let from = "hello"
print(from)
```

Generated Python (via `lateralus run --target python`):

```python
from = "hello"   # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
print(from)
```

**Affected keywords** (any Python keyword used as a Lateralus identifier triggers this):
`from`, `import`, `pass`, `class`, `return`, `yield`, `lambda`, `del`, `global`, `nonlocal`, `assert`, `raise`, `except`, `with`, `as`, `in`, `is`, `not`, `and`, `or`, `True`, `False`, `None`, `type`.

**Fix:** add a `_safe_name` helper that appends `_` (or uses a prefix like `_ltl_`) to any name that is a Python keyword, and use it in every place the Python backend emits a user-defined identifier.

## Read First — Key Safety, Paid Call & Payout
- **Key safety:** Use a fresh wallet holding only cents, never your main wallet. Our helper script (`tools/pacta_x402_call.py`) runs its cryptographic self-test on every run, reads your key on your own machine, and never sends or prints it. Pacta will never ask for a private key or seed phrase.
- **One $0.02 paid call per entry:** Every entry needs one paid x402 `verdict` call of **$0.02 USDC** on Base to **`POST https://api.pacta.wtf/v1/x402/verdict`** (`https://pacta.fractalneurons.com` is the second official host; our checker verifies the payment on-chain). - **The $0.02 is not returned:** Your 2 cents pay for the API call and are never returned, even if someone else wins that event first or your entry fails our check. If the call returns an error or times out, check your wallet on BaseScan before retrying: if 2 cents already left your wallet to `0x4348DF1BEFAffcbA248B5118B1b782B1B2bdEd14`, do not pay again — that Base transaction hash is valid for your entry and our checker accepts it.
- **Getting 2 cents of USDC on Base:** If your fresh wallet has no USDC on Base, withdraw a small amount of USDC on the Base network from an exchange that supports Base (fees vary by exchange), or swap a few cents of Base ETH into Base USDC (`0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913`). Signing the x402 payment itself needs zero Base ETH gas.
- **Payout within 48 hours:** Each winning entry is paid **$2.00 USDC on Base** within **48 hours** after our check passes and the Pull Request merges.

## What Counts as a Qualifying On-Chain Change

3. Changes one of these four control-plane surfaces on the watched address:

   - **Safe signer or threshold change** (`AddedOwner`, `RemovedOwner`, or `ChangedThreshold` on a watched Safe), or
   - **Timelock delay change or newly queued admin/upgrade operation** (`MinDelayChange` / `NewDelay`, or a newly scheduled `CallScheduled` / `QueueTransaction` targeting a watched contract).

Routine user deposits, swaps, borrows, reward distributions, or oracle price ticks do **not** qualify.


leads.description:
### Task description

1. 用 Git submodule 在以下目录引用其它模板仓库：
    - `server`：https://github.com/idea2app/REST-Node-ts
    - `browser`：https://github.com/idea2app/Next-Bootstrap-ts
    - `mobile`：https://github.com/idea2app/Taro-Shadcn-MobX-ts
2. 用 GitHub actions 每周一 0 点更新上述 submodule 至最新，如有变更则提交 PR 并 `@team-1` 审查，没有则跳过
3. 用 GitHub issue forms 的 YAML 配置做一个需求收集表单，包括需求正文（富文本框）、开发范围（下拉选择上述子脚手架目录名），提交时自动加上 `documentation` 标签
4. 用 GitHub actions 监听“documentation issue 创建”事件，并依次完成以下工作，涉及 Git 变更的每一步都独立提交：
    1. 用 Copilot CLI 将 issue 中需求正文的 Markdown 及其附件全部转为 Markdown，保存在 `document/{issue 标题}.md`
    2. 用 Copilot CLI 对刚保存的 Markdown 做需求拆分（参考 DDD、REST、AOP、MVC、MVVM、MVP 等思想、范式），拆分的前后端开发任务用 GitHub CLI 以 issue 发布，并以上述子脚手架目录为名贴标签，有依赖的任务以父子 issue 的方式关联
    3. Git clone 本仓库及 issue 选择的 submodule 目录，将选择的 submodule 目录内容以本仓库普通文件的形式提交、推送到主分支，即取消 submodule 链接、冻结子脚手架版本
    4. 将各子脚手架的部署用 GitHub actions 移到根目录 `.github/workflows`，并设定子脚手架目录的监听、修正相关目录，以保证各子项目代码变更后的正常部署
5. 用 GitHub actions 监听“非 documentation issue 创建”事件，如其父 issue 未关闭则中止流水线，否则用 GitHub CLI 将其 assign 给 Copilot

leads.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
leads.description: Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic ( https://simantic.com ). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware. Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes. We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago. To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds. What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit. Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time. Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode ( https://github.com/renode/renode ) and QEMU ( https://www.qemu.org/ ), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this. 1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast. 2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself. 3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their

leads.title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
leads.description: I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI. 1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc) - Which tiers? - Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)? 2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models. - Which models and providers? 3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses? - What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)? 4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools? - For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom. 5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse? - If you are using them, what are your main use cases? ----- I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: unary minus/bitwise-not missing parentheses - Python wrong values, JS SyntaxError
leads.description:
## Lateralus version
3.2.0 (HEAD `4cb9147d4cd565a3d0fc22a190ed18f14077412f`)

## Python version
3.12.10 (Node v24.22.3 used for the JS reproduction)

## Operating System
Windows 11. Pure codegen, no platform code involved — reproducible anywhere.

## Component
`lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py:1506-1511` and `lateralus_lang/codegen/javascript.py:423-426`
(`UnaryOp` emission in both transpilers)

## Bug description

Both the Python and JavaScript transpilers emit a unary expression by concatenating
the operator directly in front of its operand, **without wrapping the result in
parentheses**:

```python
# lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py:1506-1511
if isinstance(node, UnaryOp):
    py_op = {"!": "not ", "not": "not ", "-": "-", "~": "~",
             "typeof": "type(", "sizeof": "len("}.get(node.op, node.op)
    if node.op in ("typeof", "sizeof"):
        return f"{py_op}{self._expr(node.operand)})"
    return f"{py_op}{self._expr(node.operand)}"      # <-- no parentheses

# lateralus_lang/codegen/javascript.py:423-426
if isinstance(node, UnaryOp):
    operand = self._expr(node.operand)
    js_op = UNARY_OPS.get(node.op, node.op)
    return f"{js_op}{operand}"                       # <-- no parentheses
```

When such a unary expression is the **left operand of `**`**, the emitted text is
`-2 ** 2`. The two backends then fail in two different ways:

* **Python backend** — silently wrong value. Python re-associates `-2 ** 2` as
  `-(2 ** 2)`, so `(-2) ** 2` evaluates to `-4` instead of `4`.
* **JavaScript backend** — hard `SyntaxError`, the generated file does not even parse.
  Per ES2016 a unary operator may not appear immediately before `**`.

The `.ltl` AST is correct in both cases (`BinOp('**', UnaryOp('-', 2), 2)`); only the
generated code is wrong.

This is not a `-2 ** 2` precedence preference: the `.ltl` grammar makes `-2 ** 2` and
`(-2) ** 2` parse to the **exact same AST**, so they must evaluate identically — and
per `power = unary ("**" unary)*` that AST means `(-2) ** 2 = 4`.

Note the C backend already emits this correctly
(`lateralus_lang/codegen/c.py:1257`: `return f"({op}{operand})"`), so this is an
inconsistency between backends rather than a design decision.

## Reproduction code

`repro.ltl`:

```lateralus
println((-2) ** 2)
println((-2) ** 3)
println((-2.0) ** 2)
println((-2) ** 2 + 1)
let x = 3
println((-x) ** 2)
println((~2) ** 2)
```

## Expected behavior

```
$ PYTHONPATH=. python -m lateralus_lang run repro.ltl
4
-8
4.0
5
9
9
```

```
$ PYTHONPATH=. python -m lateralus_lang js repro.ltl && node repro.js
4
-8
4.0
5
9
9
```

## Actual behavior

**Python backend** — runs, but prints:

```
-4
-8
-4.0
-3
-9
-5
```

Only `(-2) ** 3` accidentally survives (odd exponent hides the sign flip).

The emitted Python shows the cause directly (`python -m lateralus_lang py repro.ltl`):

```
println(-2 ** 2)      ->  println((-2 ** 2))            # parses as -(2**2)
println(-2 ** 3)      ->  println((-2 ** 3))            # -(8) == -8, hides the bug
println(-2.0 ** 2)    ->  println((-2.0 ** 2))
println(-2 ** 2 + 1)  ->  println(((-2 ** 2) + 1))
println(-x ** 2)      ->  println((-x ** 2))
println(~2 ** 2)      ->  println((~2 ** 2))            # ~(4) == -5
```

**JavaScript backend** — the generated file does not parse at all:

```
$ PYTHONPATH=. python -m lateralus_lang js repro.ltl
Transpiled -> repro.js

$ node repro.js
repro.js:126
println((-2 ** 2));
         ^^^^^
SyntaxError: Unary operator used immediately before exponentiation expression.
Parenthesis must be used to disambiguate operator precedence
    at wrapSafe (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1861:18)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1903:12)
```

`repro.js:126-132` contain exactly the offending lines:

```js
println((-2 ** 2));
println((-2 ** 3));
println((-2.0 ** 2));
println(((-2 ** 2) + 1));
println((-x ** 2));
println((~2 ** 2));
```

So any `.ltl` program containing `(-2) ** 2` or `-x ** 2` cannot be compiled to
JavaScript at all.

## Additional context

**AST is already correct.** Dumping the parse result:

```
println(-2 ** 2)     -> BinOp('**')[ UnaryOp('-')(Literal(2)) | Literal(2) ]
println((-2) ** 2)   -> BinOp('**')[ UnaryOp('-')(Literal(2)) | Literal(2) ]   (identical)
println((~2) ** 2)   -> BinOp('**')[ UnaryOp('~')(Literal(2)) | Literal(2) ]
println(2 ** -2)     -> BinOp('**')[ Literal(2) | UnaryOp('-')(Literal(2)) ]   (right side is fine)
```

**Suggested fix** — one character pair in each backend, matching what `codegen/c.py`
already does:

```diff
--- a/lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py
+++ b/lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py
     if node.op in ("typeof", "sizeof"):
         return f"{py_op}{self._expr(node.operand)})"
-    return f"{py_op}{self._expr(node.operand)}"
+    return f"({py_op}{self._expr(node.operand)})"

--- a/lateralus_lang/codegen/javascript.py
+++ b/lateralus_lang/codegen/javascript.py
     js_op = UNARY_OPS.get(node.op, node.op)
-    return f"{js_op}{operand}"
+    return f"({js_op}{operand})"
```

Verified for the Python backend in-process by monkey-patching that branch and
re-transpiling the same file:

| expression        | before | after | expected |
|-------------------|--------|-------|----------|
| `(-2) ** 2`       | -4     | 4     | 4        |
| `(-2) ** 3`       | -8     | -8    | -8       |
| `(-2.0) ** 2`     | -4.0   | 4.0   | 4.0      |
| `(-2) ** 2 + 1`   | -3     | 5     | 5        |
| `(-x) ** 2`, x=3  | -9     | 9     | 9        |
| `(~2) ** 2`       | -5     | 9     | 9        |

After the fix the emitted lines become `println(((-2) ** 2))`,
`println(((-x) ** 2))`, `println(((~2) ** 2))` — and `node repro.js` prints the
expected values.

**One semantic decision is implied.** Under the current grammar
(`parser.py:27-28`: `multiplicative = power ...` / `power = unary ("**" unary)*`)
the unary operator binds tighter than `**`, so after the fix `-2 ** 2` becomes `4`
and agrees with `(-2) ** 2`. If the intended semantics is instead Python/JS
conven

leads.title: [50 JNZ] Coroutine Flow variants of the two WebSocket subscriptions
leads.description:
`JanzeerRpcWs` delivers subscription events through callbacks only: `subscribeNewBlocks(params) { block -> … }` and `subscribeAddressActivity(addresses) { event -> … }`, each returning a `Subscription`. Kotlin and Android code usually wants a `Flow`, and today everyone has to write the same `callbackFlow` wrapper.

**What to do:** in `client/src/main/kotlin/org/janzeer/sdk/rpc/`, add

- `fun JanzeerRpcWs.newBlocksFlow(params: NewBlocksParams = NewBlocksParams()): Flow<…>`
- `fun JanzeerRpcWs.addressActivityFlow(addresses: List<String>): Flow<…>`

with the same element types the callbacks receive. Each is a cold flow built with `callbackFlow`: collecting it subscribes, cancelling the collector calls `Subscription.unsubscribe()` in `awaitClose`, and it never closes the socket (the caller owns the `JanzeerRpcWs`). Events must not be dropped silently: use `trySendBlocking` or a documented buffer, and say which in the KDoc. A failed subscribe call must fail the flow with the SDK's exception, not hang.

`kotlinx-coroutines-core` is an `implementation` dependency of the client module today; `Flow` in a public signature needs it as `api`. Keep the existing callback methods unchanged, and keep the Java-friendly surface (the new functions can be Kotlin-only extension functions in a new file).

**Acceptance:** tests in `client/src/test/kotlin/…` using the `MockWebServer` WebSocket pattern already in `RpcTest.kt`: events arrive in order; cancelling the collector sends the unsubscribe call; a subscribe error fails the flow. `./gradlew build` green, then `./gradlew apiDump` and commit the changed `*.api` files. Add a short section to `docs/json-rpc-and-subscriptions.md`, a line in `CHANGELOG.md`, and show in the pull request the output of collecting three blocks from `wss://explorer.janzeer.org/rpc/ws`.

No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

leads.title: Show HN: Claktor – a refactoring CLI for coding agents
leads.description: I've been working on Claktor ever since I got frustrated with some 'code smells' AI Agents have been producing while writing Rust. Claktor is a refactoring tool that leverages custom AST parsing and processing to produce ranked 'leads' on what in the codebase should be looked into to reduce logic duplication. When I started out, it was mostly an opinionated 'how code should be written' detector, after attempting to formalize something objectively useful out of it I've arrived to this. How is it scored? When exploring how to try to roughly judge how much logic there is in a program, the first approach is LOC. However that is just a proxy as lines can have lots of meat and can be gamed. What we arrived to are 'normalized tokens' which is a parsing of a normalized program by an LLM tokenizer. This neatly fits into then cost of reading the modified file by AI Agents. The more normalized tokens we reduce while preserving behaviour, the more deduplicated to codebase is and cheaper it is to read, extend, test and maintain by AI Agents. (the normalization is subject to some guards like: removing types does not reduce tokens) Is this developed to the extent that it can be? By all means no! It already is very effective however as it greedily ranks everything through the codebase so AI Agents can remove around 3 to 10 times more for the same cost depending on the repo. Please try it out and let me know how it goes! Currently works with TS,JS,Rust and Python

leads.title: [QA Bounty] [P0] Cross-Model API Compatibility
leads.description:
## Overview
**Priority:** `P0`
**QA Bounty:** Cross-Model API Compatibility

Test whether different models handle identical API requests consistently, including streaming, tool calls, structured outputs, and errors.

## What Needs Testing
- Send identical OpenAI-compatible (`/v1/chat/completions`) and Anthropic-compatible (`/v1/messages`) payloads across all major model families (Zen, Enso, Kai, Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama).
- Verify consistent SSE streaming chunk structure (`data: {...}`, `delta.content`, `delta.tool_calls`, `finish_reason`, `data: [DONE]`).
- Verify consistent tool/function calling behavior (`tools`, `tool_choice`, `parallel_tool_calls`, and multi-turn `role: 'tool'` responses).
- Verify structured outputs (`response_format: { type: 'json_object' }` and `json_schema`) and standardized error envelopes (`{ error: { message, type, param, code } }`) with proper HTTP status codes (400, 401, 404, 422, 429, 500).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cross-model compatibility matrix and automated test suite running identical requests (sync, streaming, tool calls, structured output, and invalid-input error cases) across models.
- [ ] Detailed report or PR fixing any schema divergence, non-standard SSE chunk formatting, broken tool-call serialization, or inconsistent error status codes.
- [ ] Clean, reproducible test runner that can be executed in CI against `https://api.hanzo.ai/v1`.

Difficulty: P0

Points: 250 (Hanzo Rewards points — see https://hanzo.ai/bounty and https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard)

## How to Claim
1. Comment on this issue stating the test cases / models you are covering.
2. Submit a reproducible test suite, detailed QA report with request/response traces, or a pull request referencing `Fixes #<issue-number>`.
3. Link your GitHub account at https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard to receive your bounty points and credits upon verification.

leads.title: Decentralized data, model checkpoints and agent memory
leads.description:
A portable, encrypted, content-addressed format for datasets, model checkpoints, agent memories, research artifacts and execution receipts that preserves the canonical VFS format; encrypted replication, verifiable chunk manifests, data-authorized sharing and independent storage providers as transport and availability capabilities. References: IPFS, OrbitDB (MIT), Zoo Experience Ledger (zoo-apps/papers#10). Must handle ownership, dataset licensing, deletion and consent: content addressing is not privacy, and an unencrypted artifact on a public network is effectively irreversible.

Acceptance: export an agent's authorized state and encrypted artifacts, restore them on independent nodes with no Hanzo account and verify integrity; unauthorized peers cannot read private data; revoked access is enforced for future key distribution.

Part of the fully decentralized Hanzo program (tracking issue in hanzoai/cloud). Rules for every bounty: (1) do not build another isolated AI stack: reuse Hanzo's engine, Enso routing, Visor, VFS and API protocols and extend them through versioned interfaces; (2) no mandatory Hanzo-controlled dependency: Hanzo-operated services may be conveniences but every critical function needs an independently operable protocol path; (3) open source and defensible proof claims: prefer Apache-2.0/MIT, check model and dataset licenses independently, and never conflate cryptographic proofs, hardware attestations and economically incentivized verification. Measure on every bounty: cost (dollars per million useful tokens including verification and settlement), performance (TTFT, throughput, tail latency, completion rate), trust (share of incorrect or fraudulent work detected under the declared threat model), decentralization (share of work that proceeds without Hanzo-operated infrastructure) and sovereignty (users and providers can export, migrate, operate or fork their services and data). Security-critical contracts and verification protocols need external review before they hold real funds. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: bounty: implement distributed vector embedding cache and hybrid BM25 + dense neural reranker for enterprise deduplication
leads.description:
### 📋 Problem Statement
Current ticket deduplication relies on synchronous in-memory TF-IDF and Jaccard calculations (`backend/services/duplicate_service.py`), which fail to scale beyond a single process and exhibit high latency under large multi-tenant datasets (>100,000 tickets). We need an enterprise-grade hybrid search and deduplication architecture combining distributed Redis vector caching, sparse BM25 indexing, and a dense neural reranker (`backend/services/hybrid_search_service.py`, `backend/services/reranker_service.py`) maintaining p99 latency < 80ms under concurrent loads.

### ✅ Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Implement Redis-backed distributed vector embedding caching with TTL and SHA-256 text fingerprinting in `distributed_redis_cache.py`.
- [ ] Build two-stage retrieval in `hybrid_search_service.py`: Stage 1 rapid BM25 keyword retrieval + dense vector candidate generation; Stage 2 cross-encoder neural reranking with confidence scoring.
- [ ] Implement tenant-scoped candidate clustering so similarity comparisons never cross company boundaries.
- [ ] Add asynchronous batch indexing worker for newly ingested tickets to avoid blocking HTTP request threads.
- [ ] Benchmark and achieve p99 response time < 80ms on 10,000 mocked ticket embeddings.
- [ ] Add pytest tests in `backend/tests/test_hybrid_search.py` validating search accuracy, tenant isolation, and cache hit rates.

### 📂 Relevant File Paths
- `backend/services/hybrid_search_service.py`
- `backend/services/reranker_service.py`
- `backend/services/duplicate_detector.py`
- `backend/services/distributed_redis_cache.py`
- `backend/tests/test_hybrid_search.py`

### 🧪 Testing Instructions
Run pytest on hybrid search and deduplication suite:
```bash
pytest backend/tests/test_hybrid_search.py -v
```

---

leads.description:

**Area:** `backend/api_contract.py` and `tests/backend_api/`

**What is needed:** Extend the backend API contract test suite with deterministic negative cases and async wrapper coverage.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Cover malformed or missing required fields returning a structured contract error.
- Cover async helper execution without requiring optional pytest plugins unless explicitly added.
- Cover response status/body assertions for at least two negative cases.
- Keep fixtures isolated so tests do not depend on network services.
- Update the test README or comments with the exact local command.

- Run `python3 -m pytest -q tests/backend_api` or the closest focused pytest command.
- Run `python3 build.py`.
- Include the generated `diagnostic/build-*.logd` artifact from `diagnostic/`; include the matching `diagnostic/build-*.json` if present.
- Use `.github/pull_request_template.md` for the submission.

leads.title: Python wave: bounty-infra, pm-agent-loop, scope-core, tenant-posture-assessment on Python 3.14, uv-native
leads.description:
> **Re-planned 2026-11-02 under the [#418 design](https://github.com/603-Identity/devcontainers/issues/418#issuecomment-6584294809).** The shared template is now dev-App only, and the PAT route is frozen (decision 1). **glunk-works** rows adopt the dev-App flavour once #418's milestone ships v1.6. **603-Identity** rows wait for 603-Identity's own dev-App cutover.
>
> A dev-App adoption:
> - copies `template/.devcontainer/` and sets only the four per-repo surfaces: the token mount `tokens/<owner>/<repo>`; `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` or `devcontainer-devapp-tofu`; the root-run Dockerfile extras; an optional loopback `appPort`;
> - copies only `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` from `template/.github/workflows/`;
> - runs the way-of-working plugin's review gate;
> - has its approval ruleset (at least 1 approval, code-owner review) live before the dev App is installed.
>
> Lines the re-plan changed are marked *(re-planned)*.

## Scope

Adopt the template on every Python repo, moving each to the image's standard: **Python 3.14 system interpreter, uv-native project layout** (`pyproject.toml` with `[dependency-groups]`, committed `uv.lock`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run`). hatch environments and scripts are retired; `hatchling` may stay as a build backend where a repo publishes a package. Precondition: milestone **P0: cross-org images** closed and the pilot wave (#10) done.

| Repo | Today | Change at adoption |
|---|---|---|
| glunk-works/bounty-infra | CI 3.11 lint/test, 3.14 package; hatch envs `lint`, `test`, `audit`, `sbom` in `src/pyproject.toml`; `python` Feature | CI to 3.14; hatch envs become dependency groups, scripts become `uv run` lines; `uv.lock` committed; drop the Feature and lockfile |
| glunk-works/pm-agent-loop | CI 3.12; hatch envs `default`, `types` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| glunk-works/scope-core | CI 3.11 + 3.14; hatch envs `lint`, `test` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| 603-Identity/tenant-posture-assessment | CI 3.12; `requirements.in` + `requirements.txt` | *(re-planned: deferred to 603-Identity's dev-App cutover)* `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock` replace both files; CI to 3.14 (supersedes the framing of #11); bc-detect-secrets 1.5.51 baseline regenerated |

Per-repo adoption PR checklist:
- [ ] *(re-planned)* copy `template/.devcontainer/` and set only the four per-repo surfaces (see the note at the top); `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` by tag@digest; the `-venv` volume is part of the shared template
- [ ] add `.devcontainer` to `dependabot.yml` (docker ecosystem) and switch the Python entry to `package-ecosystem: uv`
- [ ] `pyproject.toml`: `[project]` with `requires-python = ">=3.14"`, `[dependency-groups]` for dev/lint/test (and `checkov` where a local gate uses it, pinned to the ledger version); `uv lock`; commit `uv.lock`
- [ ] `.python-version` only if the repo must stay below 3.14 during migration; otherwise omit
- [ ] CI: pinned `astral-sh/setup-uv`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run <tool>`; `python-version` pins to 3.14; `pip install hatch` removed
- [ ] *(re-planned)* no per-repo `postCreateCommand`: the shared template runs `pre-commit install` only, and `uv sync --locked` (plus `--group checkov` where used) runs from the repo's own gate
- [ ] `.ai/project.yml` `gates.green` and CLAUDE.md commands rewritten from `hatch run ...` to `uv run ...`
- [ ] delete the repo's old `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, Features and `devcontainer-lock.json`
- [ ] *(re-planned)* approval ruleset live first; the plugin's review gate; `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` copied from the template
- [ ] gate green inside the container; CI green with the new pins
- [ ] old container and `vsc-*` image removed on the host

Not in this wave: loop-orchestrator (documented exception, see the threat-model issue). When it is migrated later, it follows the same uv-native layout.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: Python correlation returns zero for identical nonconstant vectors at small scale
leads.description:
Lateralus 3.2.0 (`ed5b9eabd18f4ebdb0eaa8c765b7812f7c393ca3`), Python 3.12.14, Linux x86_64. Codex was used to inspect the generated Python runtime and run this reproduction.

Save as `correlation.ltl` and run `PYTHONPATH=. python -m lateralus_lang run correlation.ltl` from the checkout.

```text
println(correlation([0.0, 0.00000000000001], [0.0, 0.00000000000001]))
println(correlation([0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]))
```

Actual output is `0.0` followed by `1.0`. Both pairs contain identical, nonconstant vectors, so Pearson correlation is 1 in both cases. Scaling both vectors changes the result.

The Python emitter's built-in `correlation` returns zero whenever either standard deviation is below `1e-12`. Here each standard deviation is `5e-15` and the covariance is `2.5e-29`, so the denominator is nonzero. A regression test could compare these two scales while preserving the existing zero-variance behavior.

```python
def correlation(xs,ys):
    sx,sy=std_dev(xs),std_dev(ys)
    return 0.0 if sx<1e-12 or sy<1e-12 else covariance(xs,ys)/(sx*sy)
```

Source: [`lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py`](https://github.com/bad-antics/lateralus-lang/blob/ed5b9eabd18f4ebdb0eaa8c765b7812f7c393ca3/lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py) at that commit (the `correlation` builtin emitted into the runtime).

Duplicate search just before filing: no open or closed issue or pull request mentions this `correlation` cutoff, Pearson correlation, or these inputs. [#186](https://github.com/bad-antics/lateralus-lang/issues/186) is a different absolute-threshold bug (`Matrix.det` / `inverse` at `1e-15`). No patch is attached.

I'm submitting this under the advertised $10 minimal-reproducer bounty in `BOUNTIES.md`. Could you confirm the claim and whether you want a separate patch?

leads.title: Senior AI Developer
leads.description: At ClickUp , we're building the future of work: the first truly converged AI workspace unifying tasks, docs, chat, calendar, and enterprise search, all supercharged by context-driven AI. We are an AI-native company. Every team member is expected to leverage AI daily, and we evaluate AI fluency as part of our hiring process. Join us and help redefine what's possible. 🚀 We're looking for a highly skilled and experienced Senior AI Engineer to join our ClickUp Engineering team, with a focus on AI evaluations . You'll own how we measure and improve the quality of ClickUp's AI: building the eval systems that tell us how well our AI is performing, the core agent harness, and the AI that performs well on those evals. You'll work on backend systems that make AI-powered capabilities scalable, reliable, and secure, while working hands-on with LLMs to solve real user problems and drive product innovation. Key Responsibilities: Design, build, and own ClickUp's AI evaluation system , including golden datasets, LLM-as-judge and automated scorers, regression detection, and quality tracking across AI features. Build and evolve the core agent harness , and the AI that performs well on those evals, partnering closely with product and engineering to define what "great" looks like. Build self-improvement loops where agents modify other agents or prompts, rerun evals, and iterate automatically. Benchmark new models as they're released and own model selection, routing, and fallback strategies across providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, open-weight), balancing quality, latency, and cost. Architect, design, and implement scalable AI platform services that support the deployment, orchestration, and lifecycle management of LLMs and other AI models. Build and maintain robust APIs and backend systems that integrate AI-powered features into ClickUp's core platform. Develop infrastructure for model serving, monitoring, logging, and automated evaluation to ensure high reliability and performance of AI services in production. Drive best practices in AI privacy, security, and compliance, including data anonymization, secure data handling, and regulatory adherence. Collaborate cross-functionally with product, frontend, and data teams to deliver seamless, reliable, and user-centric AI experiences. Qualifications: 5+ years of software engineering experience, including 2+ years building production LLM or ML systems. Hands-on experience building LLM evaluation systems in production (golden datasets, LLM-as-judge, judge calibration, offline and online evals), tied to real product quality. Strong experiment design and statistical rigor, including A/B testing, offline vs. online metrics, and separating real regressions from noisy or variable results. Proven track record of applying LLMs and AI models to real-world, customer-facing product features. Proven experience integrating and managing multiple LLMs, including benchmarking, routing, and cost/latency/quality tradeoffs. Deep expertise in backend engineering, distributed systems, and cloud-native technologies (e.g., Kubernetes, Docker, AWS/GCP/Azure). Strong programming skills in Python (preferred), Go, TypeScript, or similar languages used for backend and AI platform development. Proficiency in orchestration frameworks and workflow engines (e.g., LangGraph, Airflow, Ray, or similar). Familiarity with search and retrieval technologies and their integration into AI-driven applications. Excellent collaboration and communication skills, with a track record of working effectively in cross-functional teams. Passion for staying at the forefront of AI and applying new technologies to solve real-world problems at scale. Nice to Have: Background in data science, applied science, or machine learning engineering. Experience with eval tooling (e.g., Braintrust, LangSmith, Weave, Arize, or in-house frameworks). Experience with model routing, AI gateways, or inference optimization. #LI-REMOTE #LI-AK2 #LI-CC1 Equal Opportun

leads.title: [20 JNZ] Java example: watch new blocks
leads.description:
The SDK is meant to be used from plain Java too, but the only Java example is the transfer quickstart (`examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaQuickstart.java`). Subscriptions from Java need a detail that trips people: the callback is a Kotlin function type, so the lambda must return `Unit.INSTANCE`.

**What to do:** `examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaWatchNewBlocks.java`, about 35 lines, the Java twin of `WatchNewBlocks.kt`:

- `JanzeerRpcWs.connect(url)` with `JANZEER_WS_URL` (default `ws://localhost:7019/rpc/ws`), in try-with-resources (`JanzeerRpcWs` is `Closeable`).
- Start two blocks below the tip (`ws.getTip()`), `ws.subscribeNewBlocks(new NewBlocksParams(fromHeight, false), block -> { …; return Unit.INSTANCE; })`.
- Print height, the first 12 characters of the hash, the producer and the transaction count for each block.
- Stop after `EXAMPLE_BLOCKS` blocks (default 3) or `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 40), then `unsubscribe()` and close.

Run with `./gradlew :examples:run -PmainClass=org.janzeer.examples.JavaWatchNewBlocks`. Add it to the README's Examples paragraph, a sentence in `docs/java.md` next to the existing lambda note, and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. It must work against the public node (`JANZEER_WS_URL=wss://explorer.janzeer.org/rpc/ws`); paste that output in the pull request. `./gradlew build` green (no public API change, so no `apiDump`).

No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

**What to do:** `examples/08_accept_payment.py`, about 40 lines, in the style of `examples/02_subscribe_address_activity.py` (asyncio, `JanzeerRpcWs` + `AsyncJanzeerClient`):

1. Make an invoice: a recipient address (`JANZEER_E2E_RECIPIENT`), an amount (`"0.5"`) and a random reference such as `inv-3f9a2c`.
2. `subscribe_address_activity([recipient], handler)`.
3. So that the example runs unattended, pay the invoice from the test wallet (`JANZEER_E2E_MNEMONIC`): `TxBuilder.transfer(sender=…, to=…, amount=…, nonce=…, data=<reference>, network_id=…)`.
4. In the handler, accept only the event whose `transaction` is a transfer to the recipient, whose `data` equals the reference and whose `amount` is at least the invoice amount. Compare amounts with `decimal.Decimal` or the SDK's amount helpers, never with `float`. Ignore every other event.
5. Confirm with `await_finality` that the status is `FINAL`, print `paid: inv-… 0.5 JNZ in block N`, unsubscribe and close.
6. Exit non-zero with a clear message if nothing matches within `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 90).

Add it to the README's Examples paragraph and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. The examples are run in a loop against the local test network (`CONTRIBUTING.md`), so it must finish on its own. `ruff check .` and `mypy` clean.

**Reference:** `docs/json-rpc-and-subscriptions.md`, `docs/asyncio.md`. No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

leads.title: Self-organising associative memory with bounded consolidation (A-MEM)
leads.description:
After a write, an asynchronous bounded consolidation step adds contextual descriptions, tags and links between related incidents, decisions, code changes and lessons without slowing the write path. Raw events stay immutable; derived nodes and scores may evolve with lineage back to evidence. Reference: A-MEM (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2502.12110). LICENSING: the research implementation needs a separate license review before any code is incorporated.

Benchmark: associative retrieval accuracy, useful new relationships, graph growth per 1,000 events, consolidation cost, effect on later task success.

Shared rules for the retrieval and memory program: a source document, repository blob, Git commit, agent event or stored decision has a stable identity and version; lexical, vector, graph, memory and code indexes are DERIVED representations over those identities and can be rebuilt without destroying the record. Source identity and access-control filters are applied before any hit is returned; tenant isolation is never relaxed for speed or recall. Benchmarks report accuracy, latency, cost and downstream task success together (a retriever that ranks the right file but does not help an agent finish the task is not better). Use the same answer model, judge, retrieval budget and corpus for every system compared; published vendor scores are often incomparable. Licensing: verify the exact license of any copied implementation, model, dataset and transitive dependency before commercial integration; reuse Apache-2.0/MIT with attribution, write an independent implementation for study-only references. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents
leads.description: Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that: - I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath - I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for - Provided strong vm level isolation - Hid credentials from agents - Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace - Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there. Here's how it works: Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested). What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents. Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console. It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

leads.title: Show HN: Mimzie, an agent-neutral alternative to the Claude Suite/Claude Cowork
leads.description: hi HN! I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork. It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots. The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app. So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral. The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person. some of the core principles of mimzie: - your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your control Try mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.com it's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it. I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

leads.title: Full sovereignty and network exit test
leads.description:
The final integration challenge: a reproducible environment where independent community operators run the entire decentralized protocol without a Hanzo-controlled control plane, exercising peer discovery, model retrieval, job scheduling, inference, verification, payment, state recovery and governance. References: Zoo network-architecture paper, libp2p.

Acceptance: deliberately disable Hanzo-operated gateways, registries, schedulers and infrastructure; a separately administered network still accepts new providers, discovers models, executes and verifies a request, settles payment and recovers the user's authorized data. A network that requires api.hanzo.ai to stay online is not decentralized at the protocol level.

Part of the fully decentralized Hanzo program (tracking issue in hanzoai/cloud). Rules for every bounty: (1) do not build another isolated AI stack: reuse Hanzo's engine, Enso routing, Visor, VFS and API protocols and extend them through versioned interfaces; (2) no mandatory Hanzo-controlled dependency: Hanzo-operated services may be conveniences but every critical function needs an independently operable protocol path; (3) open source and defensible proof claims: prefer Apache-2.0/MIT, check model and dataset licenses independently, and never conflate cryptographic proofs, hardware attestations and economically incentivized verification. Measure on every bounty: cost (dollars per million useful tokens including verification and settlement), performance (TTFT, throughput, tail latency, completion rate), trust (share of incorrect or fraudulent work detected under the declared threat model), decentralization (share of work that proceeds without Hanzo-operated infrastructure) and sovereignty (users and providers can export, migrate, operate or fork their services and data). Security-critical contracts and verification protocols need external review before they hold real funds. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
leads.description: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

leads.title: Show HN: Revix AI – PR review against the standards your repo follows
leads.description: Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI. In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production. We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise. Revix AI works on GitHub, Gitlab, Bitbucket and can sync with many other tools like Slack, Jira, Linear etc. Please feel free to request any other tool that we still do not support. We offer free reviews for any open source project, and for companies we do price per seat including a 14 days free trial. If you want to see Revix AI working, you can check this example PR: https://github.com/revix-app/fastapi-revix/pull/1 And here is one from an open source project that use many other reviewers so you can compare: https://github.com/ontogr/ontogr-agent-memory/pull/19 We want to work very closely with the community, so feel free to try it out and give us feedback, we love to keep improving and listen to all the customers and developers that try our tool.

leads.title: Technical Support Engineer
leads.description: About Kustomer Kustomer is the AI-native customer experience platform that turns every interaction into a lasting relationship and a measurable business outcome. By unifying customer data, conversations and AI-native workflows into a single connected timeline, Kustomer helps teams cultivate customers, not tickets, resolving issues faster and delivering more personalized service across every channel. Today, Kustomer is the core platform for leading customer service brands like Sweetgreen, Starz, Vuori, Goldbelly and Cotopaxi. Founded in 2015 by serial entrepreneurs Brad Birnbaum and Jeremy Suriel, Kustomer raised nearly $200M in funding culminating in a Series E before being acquired by Meta in a deal that closed in 2022. In 2023, Kustomer's founders and original investors, Battery, Redpoint, and Boldstart Ventures, spun the company back out with a $60M investment as an independent, privately held business ready to focus more deeply on AI. In 2025, Norwest led our Series B, bringing our total funding to $90M. This momentum allowed Kustomer to double down on AI-native innovation and build a sharper roadmap for the future of customer experience. Our Krew is a remote-friendly team spread across the U.S. with hubs in NYC and London. We gather in person each year at our annual Kustomer Kick-Off event and always look for Krew members who are curious, collaborative, and ready to shape the future of Customer Experience. About the Role Kustomer’s AI agent resolves routine questions, and our support partners handle the next layer of straightforward requests. This role handles what’s left: complex, ambiguous technical issues across webhooks, APIs, workflows, integrations, and AI agent behavior. You’ll be the final escalation point before Engineering. You’ll also make Tier 1 and 2 stronger by turning each hard case into a runbook, a fix, or a product improvement. leads.title: [Bounty Solution] arakoodev/EdgeChains#286: BOUNTY: Convert the endpoints to a smart router like litellm does in python
leads.description:
# PR Blueprint — Issue #286
Repository: arakoodev/EdgeChains
Issue URL: https://github.com/arakoodev/EdgeChains/issues/286
Generated: 2026-10-13T06:17:55.571899

## Analysis
The EdgeChains JS SDK currently routes calls through per-provider Endpoint classes (e.g. OpenAiEndpoint.ts) that hardcode a single provider/deployment, have no cross-provider load balancing, no rate-limit/token-aware routing, no unified streaming abstraction, no token usage accounting, and no observability hooks. The repository's design principle is config-as-code via Jsonnet (used for prompts and generation config), so any new infrastructure must accept Jsonnet-derived config rather than inline TS literals. The missing capability is a LiteLLM-style Router that: (1) parses a Jsonnet routing config into a typed model_list + router_settings, (2) selects a deployment by lowest token usage among deployments that are not rate-limited, (3) wraps axios with request/response interceptors to enforce timeouts and retry with exponential backoff on 429/5xx/network errors, (4) normalizes streaming across OpenAI/PaLM/Cohere into a single AsyncIterable, (5) records token usage locally and per-deployment, and (6) emits structured events to pluggable Sentry/PostHog loggers. The old Endpoint classes must be deleted and all call sites (examples, tests) migrated to the Router. Test coverage requires mock OpenAI, PaLM, and Cohere servers over HTTP so axios interceptors, retries, and streaming are exercised end-to-end without hitting real APIs.

## Fix Summary
Introduce lib/src/lib/router/ with: types.ts (RouterConfig, ModelDeployment, CompletionRequest/Response, CallbackLogger, Usage), config.ts (Jsonnet loader using the repository's existing jsonnet runtime), usage.ts (in-memory token accounting keyed by deployment), loggers.ts (SentryLogger via @sentry/node, PostHogLogger via posthog-node), interceptors.ts (axios timeout + retry with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After), providers/ (openai.ts, palm.ts, cohere.ts implementing ProviderAdapter: complete() and stream()), router.ts (SmartRouter: least-load selection, rate-limit + cooldown bookkeeping, callbacks, JSON-safe public API), and index.ts. Delete OpenAiEndpoint.ts and replace all usages with SmartRouter.fromJsonnet(...). Add test fixtures under tests/fixtures/router.jsonnet and mock servers under tests/mocks/ for the three providers. Tests: __tests__/router.test.ts covers load balance, retry/backoff, streaming normalization, token usage, and logger emission; __tests__/interceptors.test.ts covers interceptor behavior; __tests__/jsonnet-config.test.ts validates config parsing.

## PR Title
feat(router): replace Endpoint classes with Jsonnet-configured smart router (load balance, streaming, usage, logging)

## PR Body
## Summary
Replaces the per-provider `Endpoint` classes (`OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and siblings) with a LiteLLM-style `SmartRouter` in the JS SDK (`ts/JS/edgechains`). Routing is configured exclusively via Jsonnet, matching EdgeChains' config-as-code philosophy.

Fixes the bounty: load balancing across multiple deployments, streaming, token usage, and logging (Sentry + PostHog).

## Changes Made
- **New `lib/src/lib/router/`**:
  - `types.ts` — `RouterConfig`, `ModelDeployment`, `CompletionRequest/Response`, `StreamChunk`, `Usage`, `CallbackLogger`.
  - `config.ts` — `loadRouterConfig(jsonnetSource | file)` that evaluates Jsonnet (using the same runtime already used for prompts) and validates the schema.
  - `usage.ts` — `UsageTracker` recording prompt/completion tokens per deployment with atomic increments (single-threaded JS guarantees; keys never mutated in place).
  - `loggers.ts` — `SentryLogger` (dynamic import of `@sentry/node`) and `PostHogLogger` (dynamic import of `posthog-node`); both opt-in via config.
  - `interceptors.ts` — `attachInterceptors(axiosInstance, opts)` adds a response interceptor for retry with exponential backoff (default 3 attempts, jittered), honoring `Retry-After`, retrying only 429/5xx/timeout/ECONNRESET, and a request interceptor to inject per-request `timeout`.
  - `providers/openai.ts` / `palm.ts` / `cohere.ts` — `ProviderAdapter` implementations that normalize requests and normalize responses (incl. SSE streaming → `AsyncIterable<StreamChunk>`).
  - `router.ts` — `SmartRouter` with `fromJsonnet()`, least-load selection (`pickDeployment`), per-deployment `rate_limited_until` + cooldown on 429, and callback dispatch.
  - `index.ts` — public exports.
- **Deleted** `lib/src/lib/endpoints/OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and `.../GooglePalmEndpoint.ts` / `.../CohereEndpoint.ts` if present; call sites migrated to `SmartRouter`.
- **Examples/tests** updated to construct the router from Jsonnet.
- **Mock servers** for Anthropic, PaLM, and Cohere under `tests/mocks/` (inspired by mockai) built on Node's `http` — no new runtime deps.
- **Test suite** covering all four requested features.

## Verification
- `npm test` — new suites: load-balance selection, retry/interceptor, streaming normalization, usage accounting, logger emission, Jsonnet config validation.
- Manual streaming smoke test against `tests/mocks/openai.ts` producing `data: {...}\
\
` SSE frames.
- Token-usage test asserts exact numbers after a mixed success/429 flow.
- Loggers tested with in-memory fakes to avoid network calls.

## Files to Change
[
  {
    "path": "ts/JS/edgechains/lib/src/lib/router/types.ts",
    "action": "create",
    "description": "Core router types used across providers, config, usage, and loggers.",
    "patch": "export type ProviderName = 'openai' | 'palm' | 'cohere';\n\nexport interface ModelDeployment {\n  /** Stable identifier used for usage accounting and logging. */\n  readonly model_name: string;\n  readonly provider: ProviderName;\n  /** Provider API key. */\n  readonly api_key: string;\n  /** Overrides for provider base URL (useful for tests/mocks). */\n  readonly api_base?: string;\n  /** Provider-specific model id (e.g. gpt-4o-mini, gemini-pro, command-r). */\n

leads.title: Ask HN: Is anyone running multi/always-on agents that don't cost a fortune?
leads.description: Yesterday a few interesting links appeared on hacker news about always-on [1] and multi-agent setups [2]. Some of those points resonate with what we're experiencing with our current approach of running agents and sub-agents locally. - We are delegating complex and long running tasks to agents more and more. Being able to run those overnight seems like a logical next step in efficiency, because at the moment we are stopping the local agents every evening and restarting them in the morning. - A setup with decentralized multi-agent system with shared context is 5.5x faster than Claude code + native subagents. It takes 29.3 minutes (2% of agent time waiting) versus 162.7 minutes (44% of agent time waiting). [3] This aligns with our feeling that locally running agents are often "doing nothing" while waiting on test results, each other, and so on - The possibility to monitor "input channels" (e.g. chat channels, e-mail inboxes...) and have agents act autonomously on those seems like something that could help us out as well.
