leads.title: AI is coming for accounting after coding
leads.description: Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. writing contracts is where an LLM shines, it's basic building blocks are formal words. Formal is the key term here. Accounting if different. More precise, it tolerates less mistakes. The rules that govern it are much less open to intrepretation. In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future. In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate. It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. Accounting follows the same power law as football. In a 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad journal entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal: 1. In those two, a task would not be ruined by a single mistake in the system. An app would run fine with a couple of bugs if the system design was decent. A contract would still be enforceable with an additional weak sentence in most cases. But in accounting, 1 digit error would ruin the entire balance sheet. 2. The cost of making a mistake. Worst case scenario, the system goes down for a couple of hours, you might lose a case because of a bad contract. But losing track of the financials is a different story, it can easily destroy the whole company. 3. Trust is harder to establish with accounting. You can outsource legal without understanding much about the law. But if you outsource accounting without understanding the numbers; you are toast. Also, all the major labs are going after it soon, margins are going down fast. Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl crashes on Python target (float mid from `/ 2` and undefined `hash_fnv1a_64`)
leads.description:
### Summary
`stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl` fails at runtime on the Python target in two places:
1. **Float division in binary search (`lookup` line 93 & `lookup_n` line 112):** `let mid = (lo + hi) / 2` compiles to Python true division (`/`), producing a `float` (e.g. `1.5`) and crashing `r["points"][mid]` with `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float`. (Same pattern in `stdlib/merkle.ltl:106` with `index = index / 2`.)
2. **Undefined `hash_fnv1a_64`:** `consistent_hash.ltl` imports `hash`, which exports `fnv1a_64` rather than `hash_fnv1a_64`.

### Reproduction
```python
from pathlib import Path
from lateralus_lang.compiler import Compiler, Target

ch = Path("stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
src = ch.replace("import hash", "fn hash_fnv1a_64(s: str) -> int { return len(s) * 2654435761 }") + '\nlet r = new_ring(3)\nadd_node(r, "n1")\nprintln(lookup(r, "k1"))\n'
r = Compiler().compile_source(src, target=Target.PYTHON)
exec(r.python_src, {})
```

### Actual
`TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float`

leads.title: [50 JNZ] Nix package (flake) for jz
leads.description:
NixOS and Nix users cannot run the released `jz` binary directly (it is a normal glibc binary), and there is no Nix package.

**What to do:** a `flake.nix` at the repository root plus `packaging/nix/package.nix`:

- `packages.x86_64-linux.default` and `packages.aarch64-linux.default`: fetch `jz-<ver>-linux-x64.tar.gz` / `jz-<ver>-linux-arm64.tar.gz` from the GitHub release with `fetchurl` and the hash from that release's `SHA256SUMS`, patch the binary with `autoPatchelfHook` (it needs only glibc and zlib), install `bin/jz` and the three shell completions with `installShellFiles` (generated by `jz completion bash|zsh|fish`).
- `packages.<darwin systems>.default`: wrap `jz-<ver>.jar` with a JDK 17+ (`makeWrapper`), as the Homebrew formula in `packaging/homebrew/jz.rb` does. There is no native macOS binary yet.
- `apps.default` so that `nix run github:janzeerOrg/janzeer-cli -- info` works.
- `meta`: description, homepage https://janzeer.org, licence Apache-2.0, `sourceProvenance = [ binaryNativeCode ]` (and `binaryBytecode` for the jar), `mainProgram = "jz"`.
- Version and hashes in one place at the top of `package.nix`, so a release changes three lines. Commit `flake.lock`.

**Acceptance:** `nix build` and `nix flake check` pass on x86_64-linux; `./result/bin/jz version` and `./result/bin/jz info` work; `nix run . -- block tip` works. leads.title: Show HN: Headwig - Run and test parallel AI agents without Git worktrees
leads.description: Hey HN! I am Harsh, been developing software for quite sometime now. Since agents came into my local SD workflow I had been facing a bottleneck. Event though agents are great in working parallelly, testing their changes and iterating is a pain. (Brain, storage & memory overhead) We all use Git worktrees to code in parallel. But how do we test those changes? Still linearly. Or patched up multi-environment setup. And what if you have multiple microservices in an application? How do you test different combinations? I am building Headwig to help me with this. It lets me run multiple agents on my app, isolate their changes across services, and test and iterate on each one independently, even while other agents are working, without the storage overhead of duplicating workspaces for every task. I've been using it for my own webapp, and I want you guys to look at the workflow and see if it makes sense and give me any suggestions or feedback. https://harsh-kr-jha.github.io/headwig/

leads.description:
> **Payment:** 本项目**不付钱**。`zero-bounty` / `$0` 意味着只有信用回报：merge credit、贡献者图、 > Hall of Fame。真正的赏金只存在于有人用 Opire 的 `/reward ` 资助的 issue 上。见 > `JOIN.md` § "Bounties & payment"。 ## 背景 README 目前只有三种语言：English（canonical）、日本語、简体中文。仓库的语料、客户端插件和 MCP 工具已经在讲多种语言的故事（`locale/` 有 en/ja/ko/zh-CN），但**入口文档**没有跟上——一个韩语或 西班牙语的 agent 作者，第一屏看到的是自己读不懂的 README。 这个任务就是补这个缺口：**一种语言一个 PR**，从当前 `main` 的 `README.md` 完整翻译。 ## 可选语言（任选一种，先到先得） | 语言 | 文件名 | 备注 | |---|---|---| | 한국어 | `README.ko.md` | `locale/` 里已有 ko，术语可以对齐 | | Español | `README.es.md` | | | Français | `README.fr.md` | | | Deutsch | `README.de.md` | | | Português (Brasil) | `README.pt-BR.md` | 地区变体请带 `BR` | | Русский | `README.ru.md` | | | 其他 | 先在本 issue 里问一句 | 避免两个 PR 撞同一种语言 | ## 硬性验收标准（AC） 全部满足才会合；任何一条不满足都会被打回，而不是"先合了再补"。 **AC1 · 文件与范围** - 新文件放在仓库根目录，命名 `README..md`（语言代码按上表；地区变体用 `pt-BR` 这种写法）。 - 内容是从**当前 `main`** 的 `README.md` 的完整翻译：不删章节、不合并章节、不"摘要式翻译"。 - 一个 PR 只加**一种**语言。 **AC2 · 徽章必须与 `README.md` 完全对齐** - 同一组 ``，顺序一致；`alt` 文本可以翻译，**href 一个字符都不能改**。 - 新增语言必须注册进 `tests/test_readme_badge_parity.py` 的 `TRANSLATIONS` 元组。 - 自测： ```console $ python3 -m pytest tests/test_readme_badge_parity.py -q ``` **AC3 · 语言切换行** - 新 README 顶部要有与 `README.md` 相同的 `
` 语言列表； - 同时更新 `README.md`、`README.ja.md`、`README.zh-CN.md` 三处，把新语言加进去（顺序固定： English | 日本語 | 简体中文 | <你的语言>）； - 四个链接互相可达（点进去都能打开）。 **AC4 · 不要翻译的东西** - 代码块、命令、URL、文件路径、环境变量、徽章 href、图片路径——**原样保留**； - 专有名词按现有译法：`MCP`、`DCO`、`intake`、`lesson`、`node`、`E0–E4` 不翻译（或在首次出现时 用括号给译名）；与 `README.zh-CN.md` / `README.ja.md` 的既有译法保持一致。 **AC5 · 不许写死数字** - README 里的课程数**只能来自 shields 徽章**（`data/badges/lessons.json`），不许手写 "940 lessons" 之类的总数——`tests/test_lesson_count_ssot.py` 会拦。 - 自测： ```console $ python3 -m pytest tests/test_lesson_count_ssot.py -q $ python3 scripts/sync_lesson_count.py --check ``` **AC6 · 图片与资源预算** - 图片引用与 `README.md` 一致（`promotional/*`），不新增 > 1 MB 的图片； - 新文件要加进 `tests/test_readme_asset_budget.py` 的 `READMES` 列表。 - 自测： ```console $ python3 -m pytest tests/test_readme_asset_budget.py tests/test_readme_scope_section.py -q ``` **AC7 · 翻译质量** - 逐段校对，**不接受未校对的机翻**；明显的机翻腔（词序、量词、连接词生硬）会被要求返工。 - 术语一致：同一术语全文只用一种译法；首次出现可括注原文。 - 中文/日文 README 里的"诚实边界"段落（E4、benchmark 暂停、0 赏金）必须保义，不许美化或省略。 **AC8 · 提交与流程** - 每个提交带 `Signed-off-by`（`git commit --signoff`），DCO 检查必须绿； - PR 标题：`docs(readme): add translation`； - PR 描述里贴出上面四条自测命令的输出； - 先在本 issue 回 `/try` 认领，**同一时间一个开放 PR**；两周没有进展会在 issue 里问一次，仍无进展则释放。 ## 怎么开始 ```console $ git clone https://github.com/Ikalus1988/MisakaNet.git $ cd MisakaNet $ git checkout -b docs/readme- # 翻译 README.md → README..md，改三处语言切换行、两个测试里的文件列表 $ python3 -m pytest tests/test_readme_badge_parity.py tests/test_readme_asset_budget.py \ tests/test_readme_scope_section.py tests/test_lesson_count_ssot.py -q $ python3 scripts/sync_lesson_count.py --check $ git commit --signoff -am "docs(readme): add translation" ``` ## 参考 - 三种现有 README：`README.md`、`README.ja.md`、`README.zh-CN.md` - 徽章一致性：`tests/test_readme_badge_parity.py`（文件头解释了为什么必须逐一对齐） - 资源预算：`tests/test_readme_asset_budget.py` - 计数 SSOT：`scripts/sync_lesson_count.py`、`tests/test_lesson_count_ssot.py` - 零赏金制度：`JOIN.md` § "Bounties & payment"

leads.title: Ask HR: Systems Engineering's Senior Pipeline Crisis
leads.description: The modern software industry is engineering its own talent famine. In mission-critical systems programming—especially within the C++ ecosystem—companies are dismantling entry-level pathways while demanding senior-level proficiency from day one. By treating engineering talent purely as a resource to be acquired from the market rather than cultivated from within, corporations are creating an unsustainable knowledge vacuum that threatens the long-term maintainability of global software infrastructure. This systemic breakdown is driven by four interconnected bottlenecks. 1. The Myth of the Zero-Risk Junior C++ sits at the foundation of critical infrastructure: autonomous systems, high-frequency trading platforms, game engines, and operating systems. Because code executes so close to hardware with manual memory management, companies fear that hiring inexperienced engineers introduces unmanageable stability and security risks. However, this risk-averse stance ignores the foundational role of structured code review and mentorship. When senior engineers review junior code, they do not just check syntax; they evaluate systemic logic, memory lifecycles, and architecture. By treating code review as an administrative burden rather than a primary vehicle for knowledge transfer, organizations lock out developing engineers under the false assumption that entry-level hires are inherently unmanageable risks. 2. The Economic Short-Termism of Mentorship Engineering management increasingly views senior developer time through the lens of short-term feature delivery. Because supervising a junior requires context switching and time investment from senior staff, companies calculate a temporary drop in senior output as a net negative for the quarter. This short-sighted economic model creates a classic free-rider problem: every company wants to hire seniors, but no company wants to invest the time required to produce them. Organizations optimize for immediate quarterly balance sheets while borrowing heavily against their future technical capacity. 3. The Fallacy of AI and Automated Tooling as Onboarding Substitutes To bypass human mentorship, the industry has leaned heavily on static analyzers, dynamic sanitizers, and AI code generation. While tools like AddressSanitizer or Valgrind are essential for catching runtime violations, and AI models can generate syntax boilerplate, neither can replace senior guidance. Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate syntactically convincing C++ code that masks subtle data races, lifetime issues, or cache-unfriendly patterns under multi-threaded loads. Relying on automated tools or AI output without experienced human architectural oversight leaves teams vulnerable to silent, catastrophic failures that only deep domain experience can prevent. 4. The Looming Senior Drought The consequence of this hiring gatekeeping is an unavoidable demographic and skills crisis: * Knowledge Hoarding: High-level engineering roles remain restricted to a shrinking group of veterans who entered the field when companies still trained entry-level talent. * Infrastructure Fragility: Massive legacy codebases—built over decades—are becoming increasingly complex just as the pipeline of engineers capable of maintaining them dries up. * Retirement Vacuum: As current senior architects retire or move into executive management over the next decade, companies will find a missing generation of engineers who were never given the professional environment to develop senior-level intuition. The Path Forward Resolving this crisis requires engineering leadership to recognize that seniority is an outcome of organizational investment, not a static commodity to be bought off job boards. Without dedicated onboarding pipelines, low-risk pairing models, and explicit time budgets for senior-led code review, the systems engineering ecosystem risks starving its core infrastructure of the expertise needed to sustain it.

leads.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

leads.title: [Bounty $2,000] Restore OpenVLA execution and action correctness
leads.description:
# 📝 Background

OpenVLA (openvla/openvla-7b) in models/experimental/openvla has reported runtime failures on a single Wormhole N150 and produces robot actions that do not align with the Hugging Face reference. The report attributes the output errors to three issues: missing SigLIP positional embeddings, missing Q/K weight permutation, and an off-by-one error when assembling the action-token sequence.

The submitted fixes were tested on N150. This bounty is for a working, tested OpenVLA path—not a performance optimization or a real-robot benchmark.

# 🎯 What Success Looks Like

Submit one PR that satisfies all criteria below:
- OpenVLA initializes and runs end-to-end inference on a single Wormhole N150 using the repository’s supported environment, without manual runtime patches.
- SigLIP patch embeddings include the checkpoint’s positional embeddings, and a deterministic regression test compares the resulting features with the Hugging Face reference.
- Q/K weights are mapped into the layout expected by the OpenVLA attention/RoPE path. A regression test compares intermediate language-model outputs with the Hugging Face reference.
- predict_action returns the action tokens in the correct sequence, including the first action token produced during prefill; it does not shift action dimensions or use the EOS token as an action dimension.
- Automated regression coverage checks SigLIP features, early-layer logits or hidden states, and decoded actions against a fixed reference checkpoint and fixed inputs. Document the reference environment and the numerical tolerances; agree those tolerances with the OpenVLA owner before final review. Include at least one stable case that checks token ordering explicitly.
- The N150 end-to-end test and relevant existing OpenVLA tests pass. Provide the exact commands and test results in the PR.
- No unrelated model behavior or test failures are introduced. Performance optimization, N300/T3K/Blackhole validation, and a LIBERO/Bridge or other robot benchmark are out of scope.

# 💡 Problem to Solve

The report identifies three correctness defects:

- The SigLIP path applies patch embeddings without adding the checkpoint’s pos_embed before the encoder.
- OpenVLA’s Hugging Face-to-Meta key mapping renames weights but does not apply the Q/K permutation used by the TT-Transformers loader for the configured RoPE layout.
- The action decoder keeps the prefill-produced first action token separately, then returns later decode tokens as the action sequence, shifting the action dimensions and allowing EOS to be interpreted as the gripper action.
- It also reports seven N150 runtime blockers on the reported baseline (07fac6de536):
- Transformers accesses language_model before initialization in _supports_sdpa.
- post_init calls tie_weights with an unsupported argument.
- generate passes a cache object that fails an assertion.
- OpenVLA passes the string "prefill" where the TT-Transformers API expects Mode.PREFILL.
- Prefill RoPE uses the row-major cosine matrix instead of the prefill-specific slice.
- The timm version check rejects a version allowed by the declared dependency range.
- The test requests FABRIC_1D on a one-chip mesh, which is rejected by current fabric initialization.
- Before opening the bounty, confirm which reported runtime failures still reproduce on current main; remove any already-resolved items from the final scope. The reported pre-existing test_siglip_intermediate failure is not part of this bounty unless the owner confirms it is required to validate these fixes.

leads.title: Simplify the Chrome extension to a chatbot with in-browser capabilities
leads.description:
## User story

As a customer, I want the Hanzo Chrome extension to feel like a simple in-browser chatbot — similar to Claude in Chrome — so I can ask about the current page without wading through a complicated toolbar.

## What's wrong today

The extension is too complicated for non-technical customers. The default surface should be a chatbot with in-browser capabilities (read the current tab, work with the page). Extra features should live in the extension settings, with an option to pin the ones a customer actually uses onto the main interface.

This is not the same as the small visual cleanups in #7 and #8.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The default extension UI is a chatbot that can work with the current tab (read, select, and act in the page).
- [ ] Additional features are moved into the extension's settings.
- [ ] Customers can optionally pin chosen features onto the main extension interface.
- [ ] First-run install and use do not require understanding the local daemon, fabric, or unpacking a zip if a store listing is available; if a store listing is not ready, the install path is still a few clicks with plain-language instructions.

## Source

Customer feedback. Keep this issue free of personal names, phone numbers, keys, and secrets.

Growth paths: Joining ElevenLabs means joining a dynamic team with countless opportunities to drive impact - beyond your immediate role and responsibilities. Learning & development : ElevenLabs proactively supports professional development through an annual discretionary stipend. Social travel : We also provide an annual discretionary stipend to meet up with colleagues each year, however you choose. You'll balance people leadership, strategic direction, and hands-on customer impact - driving excellence in post-sales outcomes and ensuring your team consistently delivers measurable value to customers and the business. You will: Lead, coach, and develop a high-performing AM team, owning team and regional NRR performance, customer retention, and expansion goals. Act as a player-coach: directly manage priority accounts, join key customer conversations, and model best-in-class success practices. Lead by example in complex post-sales and renewal cycles, unblocking issues, driving adoption, and identifying expansion opportunities. leads.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
leads.description: I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. leads.title: Show HN: OpenWants – A Simulated City Where AI Agents Handle Residents Needs
leads.description: Iv'e been working on this for a while. Most of the effort went into what i call "sophisticated simplicity", keep the idea in the smallest version that still works. This one is a bit personal. it can feel like some sci-fi thing, but i've been obsessed with it for a very long time. its not a "business" that you used to see here speak about moat or tam, its more like an experiment, a way of me to take one question seriously and see where it leads and if there are others like me out there. AI models are on a path to keep getting better and better, personal ai agents are spreading fast, and we're starting to see "ghost" agents that handle the things for people they don't want to do themselves. the question i keep coming back to is this: if every one of us has a powerful brain in our pocket, do we still need all the infrastructure we built to connect people's needs? im talking about those services like uber,airbnb,indeed,doordash,tinder,zillow,amazon and many more. or would agents just need one shared place to find each other, and that's it? So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example: A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free" A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. Another thing i checked is with my friends: we took 3 agents, one for each one, and gave them different sophisticated scenarios, and the agents handled the scenarios in a way i couldn't have imagined. you can try it by yourself, the product is fully functioning, and you can just copy-paste the skill and test it also with your friends. That's it, you can see it in the simulated city it happens like magic over and over again. the list of the city is in the simulator itself and also using my real product behind it openwants.com the repo is in https://github.com/openwants/maplehill -- technically, it's surprisingly simple. every agent publishes an md file describing a "want". other agents find it, message each other, and update the file live or remove it from the list. the file holds everything needed, all in free text: what's wanted, the live location, geofence for where its needed. all those algorithms built over years to connect us are no longer needed. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

征集 HarnessClaw 的体验测评（第二期，编号备注 #2）—— 任一场景均可，例如：

**内容要求**：

- 字数不限，建议 300 字以上，有真实使用上下文
- 可以中英文，可以加截图 / 录屏链接
- 拒绝 AI 一键生成的空泛吹捧或纯负面情绪宣泄 —— 重点是「具体场景 + 你的真实感受 + 可复现的细节」

为了保证奖励真正发给「用过 HarnessClaw 的人」，PR 需要同时满足以下条件，否则不予接受：

1. **真实使用证据**（必选其一）
   - 在测评中贴出至少一次完整 chat / agent / skill / sub-agent 调度的截图或短视频；
   - 或提供本地 session 记录的 session ID + 简短上下文摘录（路径见 `~/.harnessclaw/db/harnessclaw.db`）；
   - 或提供安装某个 skill 后的实际产出片段（命令、文件、回复均可）。
   - 仅跑 `yarn install` / `yarn build` / `yarn dev` 启动窗口 **不算「使用」**。
2. **贡献形态**：不接受 `docs/reviews/<author>.md` 这种空文档型 PR。可选形式：
   - 写到个人博客 / 飞书 / 公众号 / 知乎等平台，在 issue 评论里贴链接 + 摘要；
   - 或直接把测评正文贴在本 issue 评论中；
   - 或针对仓库做**有实质内容**的改动（文档勘误、bug 修复、功能改进等）并附上简短测评。
3. **账号信誉**：不接受过去 30 天内在 ≥ 3 个无关 bounty repo（不同主题 / 不同组织 / 不同生态）都开过 PR 的账号。
4. **AI 辅助透明披露**：若测评内容由 AI 辅助生成，须在 PR 描述顶部显式声明，并附上：

leads.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
leads.description: Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. leads.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
leads.description: Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ( https://laminar.sh/blog ) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ( https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr ). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

leads.title: Show HN: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar
leads.description: Hello! I'm Marc. I've built "Nunya", which is a sort of "digital privacy screen". It redraws text to make it readable when looking at your monitor or phone from a normal distance, while making it hard to read by someone who might be looking over your shoulder. It's based on “hybrid images” like the famous Einstein/Monroe image (from the paper at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1141911.1141919 ) and I thought it'd make a great way to mask text on your phone that you don't want someone nearby reading. I particularly spent time on the transition - I wanted the text to be incredibly legible when close, but incredibly illegible when being far, and tried to optimise for a minimal transition between the two. Demos can be seen at my site for it here: https://usenunya.com I first released this over ten years ago as "PrivacyMessage" (my app names have definitely improved) when Apple first allowed iMessage apps. This was my first app geared towards the general market as I've spent the last 13 years developing iOS apps for a fairly niche market. I'm happy to have brought it back as “Nunya”, and have currently made it available in three forms: - Nunya for Messages (iPhone) I first remade my iMessage app and gave it a bit more polish. It's free for 5 sends, and then $4.99 for a permanent unlock. - Potfolio (iPhone) I then figured Nunya would make for a great flagship feature in a "wealth tracking" finance app I was already working on, so anyone who might glance at your phone when on public transport can't quite see your bank balances. It's currently free (though I might add some new features with IAPs to it later). - Nunya for Chrome A friend then suggested it'd make for a great Chrome extension to be used on all sites. It's free to hide money amounts, and £10 (around $13) to unlock it to work with more (bank details, bitcoin addresses, etc). You can try it here: https://usenunya.com/chrome This is my first real attempt at making apps for a wider market. It's also my very first Chrome extension, and I'm not entirely sure how best to price each of these, nor how to best gate their features. I don't particularly like subscriptions if I can avoid them. I'm curious to hear any thoughts. Particularly: do you think these pricing models are reasonable? I also wonder if Nunya would make for a good feature elsewhere. With more staff working remotely who might be in transit or in cafes, I can imagine businesses could be keen for their staff to use it on more sensitive data. Does that seem plausible? Thanks all.

leads.description:
## The gap — 35 RTC

The node's table has the 68000 family at **2.2x–3.0x**, the classifier knows `68000`/`68020`/`68030`/`68040`/`mc68`/`m68k`, the Linux miner maps `m68k` to family `M68K`, and we ship a 61-hash database of emulator ROMs (`node/rom_fingerprint_db.py`) precisely so that real Amigas and 68K Macs can be told apart from UAE and Basilisk II. **No 68K machine has ever attested** because nothing in `miners/` runs on AmigaOS, TOS or System 6/7. No open bounty covers 68K (searched this board 2026-11-06).

## Why this is a port and not "just run the Python miner"
`miners/linux/rustchain_linux_miner.py` detects ``m68k`` via `platform.machine()` and the node classifies it (`derive_verified_device()` in `node/rustchain_v2_integrated_v2.2.1_rip200.py` ~L3056) — so on a modern Linux with Python 3.11 it may already attest. That is not this bounty. The hardware Proof of Antiquity exists to reward runs on AmigaOS 1.3–3.x, Atari TOS/MiNT, or Mac OS System 6–8 (68K) on the original hardware, where there is no Python 3.11 and often no TLS. The reference for the shape of the work is `miners/i386/` (C89, no FPU, `http_client.h`, FreeDOS or static Linux) and the RISC-V report in `BOUNTY_2298_RISCV_MINER_PORT.md`.

## Deliverable
A PR to `Scottcjn/Rustchain` adding `miners/m68k/`:

1. A miner that builds and runs **on AmigaOS 1.3–3.x, Atari TOS/MiNT, or Mac OS System 6–8 (68K) on the original hardware** with the toolchain you name (pinned version). Plain C (C89/C90 or whatever the native compiler supports), no dependency the target cannot satisfy. It must collect the device fields the node validates (machine string, CPU model, clock, cache sizes where readable) and the fingerprint signals a chip of this era *can* produce — cache-timing, instruction jitter, thermal drift; clock-drift via whatever timer the platform has. Honest reporting: if a check cannot run on the hardware, send it as not-run, never fabricated.
2. Attestation submitted to a node. Because the target has no modern TLS, the supported path is the LAN proxy pattern in `miners/README.md` (plain HTTP to a proxy you run on a modern box that forwards to the node over HTTPS). Document it; do not ship a weakened-TLS hack.

You may occasionally visit a GoDaddy office to meet with your team for events or meetings. Join Our Team… GoDaddy's Global Storage Engineering team operates one of the largest Ceph environments in the industry, powering the object, block, and file storage platforms that underpin hosting, applications, internal infrastructure, and next-generation AI/HPC workloads. If you're passionate about distributed systems, large-scale storage architecture, and solving complex reliability challenges, you'll work on infrastructure that few engineers ever experience. At GoDaddy, Ceph isn't a side project — it's a critical platform. Our environment spans 80+ production clusters, 20,000+ OSDs, and approximately 300 PB of raw storage capacity, supporting tens of billions of objects across multiple continents. The scale demands deep technical expertise in storage architecture, automation, observability, and performance engineering. As a Senior Site Reliability Engineer, you'll be a key technical owner of the platform, responsible for maintaining reliability, driving operational excellence, and influencing the future evolution of our storage ecosystem. You'll tackle challenging production problems, develop automation that operates at massive scale, contribute to architectural decisions, and collaborate with some of the industry's most experienced Ceph engineers. Lead storage lifecycle initiatives including cluster expansions, hardware refreshes, software upgrades, OpenStack integrations, and large-scale migration projects. Your Experience Should Include… 5+ years operating large-scale Linux infrastructure with significant experience supporting distributed storage systems in production environments. 2+ years hands-on Ceph administration including OSD, MON, MDS, and RGW operations, CRUSH map management, pool design, placement groups, and performance troubleshooting. Strong understanding of Linux internals, storage architecture, networking, filesystems, block devices, and performance analysis under production workloads. Experience developing operational automation and tooling with Python, Shell, and configuration management platforms such as Ansible, SaltStack, Puppet, or Chef. Proven incident response expertise, including production troubleshooting, root-cause analysis, postmortem creation, and implementation of durable corrective actions. You Might Also Have… Advanced Ceph expertise across RGW Multisite, CephFS, RBD Mirroring, erasure coding, and large-scale cluster design. Experience integrating storage platforms with OpenStack (Cinder, Nova, Neutron, Swift) or Kubernetes storage technologies (CSI, StorageClasses, Rook). Familiarity with modern observability platforms including Prometheus, Mimir, Loki, Grafana, and enterprise monitoring architectures. Experience planning and executing petabyte-scale storage migrations, capacity expansion programs, and storage hardware

leads.title: Senior Revenue Forecasting & Operations Business Partner
leads.description: Caylent is an AI-first cloud services company that helps organizations turn ambitious ideas into meaningful business impact. As an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner and a charter member of Anthropic’s Claude Partner Network, we combine deep expertise in AWS, artificial intelligence, and Anthropic’s Claude platform to help customers modernize their technology, build intelligent products, and move AI from experimentation into production. Our capabilities span generative and agentic AI, cloud migration and modernization, cloud-native application development, data and analytics, DevOps, managed services, security and compliance, and customer experience transformation. At Caylent, our people always come first. We are a fully remote global company with employees in Canada, the United States and Latin America. We celebrate the culture of each of our team members and foster a community of technological curiosity. Come talk to us to learn more about what it means to be a Caylien! The Mission We are seeking a Senior Revenue Forecasting & Operations Business Partner to own Caylent’s revenue forecast and the operational data that feeds it, and to act as the finance partner to our Sales and Delivery leadership. Reporting to the Director of Finance, you will turn signed SOWs, staffing plans, and billing schedules into a forecast leadership can rely on, and explain the variance when actuals land. This is a hands-on role with high visibility to the CFO and the executive team. You will work daily with senior leaders across Sales, Delivery, Resource Management, and Accounting, challenging assumptions, influencing decisions, and translating financial trade-offs into clear recommendations they can act on. As we grow, you will also help integrate acquired entities into our forecasting, reporting, and systems. Your Assignment Revenue Forecasting and Finance Business Partner Own the monthly and quarterly revenue forecast across all entities (US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico) and subsidiaries, and maintain a rolling 12-month forecast that supports the annual budget and reforecast cycles. Build the forecast bottom-up from signed SOWs, change orders, staffing plans, and billing schedules, and reconcile it top-down to the Salesforce pipeline and bookings. Forecast by revenue type : time and materials, fixed fee, managed services, and AWS-funded engagements. Model backlog burn, utilization, and bench impact on revenue, and flag engagements at risk of under-delivery or overrun. Deliver a monthly forecast vs. actuals package with variance explained by engagement, practice, and entity. Business Partnering Act as the trusted finance partner to Sales, Delivery, and Resource Management leaders, joining their forecast, pipeline, and staffing reviews on a recurring basis. Partner on deal and SOW structuring (pricing, fee model, AWS funding) before signature, not only after. Challenge assumptions (pipeline conversion, utilization, staffing, deal structure) with data, and influence decisions. Translate financial trade-offs (margin, cash, risk) into clear recommendations for senior, non-finance stakeholders. Systems, Data & Reporting Be the Finance owner of revenue data across Salesforce, the PSA or time tracking system, and the ERP; define the fields and controls that keep them in sync. Build and maintain forecast models and dashboards with full traceability from reported numbers back to source records. Automate recurring reporting where practical (Google Sheets, Apps Script, SQL, BI tooling, or AI tools). Document revenue operations processes and controls to support audit and month-end close. What Success Looks Like First 30 days: Understand the forecast end to end and map every active engagement to its fee structure, billing schedule, funding terms, and staffing plan. First 90 days: Own the monthly forecast and deliver the first forecast vs. actuals package with variance explained by engagement; establish regular cadences with Sales and Delivery leadership

leads.title: FinOps Data Engineer
leads.description: About the Role We're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company. This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week. What You'll Be Responsible For In this role, you'll: Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation. Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on. Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online. Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match. Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on. Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review. Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit. Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read. You Might Be a Good Fit If You Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics. Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing). Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb. Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash. Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex). Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work. Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required. leads.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
leads.description: Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino ( https://kino.ai ). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052 ). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ( https://regressions.net ). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning

leads.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
leads.description: Hi HN, Mark here. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up. Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood. Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT- ) from code tasks (SUB- ) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free. Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves. "nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry. One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly. Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now. Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

leads.title: Show HN: ReVault – new secure archive format
leads.description: reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use. I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI. It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings. A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively. - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata. - Zstd compression. - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible. We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools. The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/ reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift. Within a lockbox you can store: - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks. - Variables. - Forms. Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions. reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions. It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this. There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose: lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox lbx mybox open --duration 1h lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out: lbx session default mybox lbx var get KEY You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes: lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project lbx store.lbox mirrors update The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast. Recovery Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted. Sharing An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it. reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental. OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits. To publish your default profile's public key: lbx vault profiles email you@example.com lbx vault profiles publish Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key: lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name> Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel: lbx vault profiles fingerprint Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox: lbx access grant alice You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice. To install the CLI and get started: cargo install revault_cli lbx vault init lbx completion install Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues: lbx doctor The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories. I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

# [Bounty] Answer the 3 linked question(s)

## Context

These intakes ask about something no lesson covers. Measured through the production retrieval path (BM25 plus the IDF-weighted relevance floor), every one of them returns `no_match` — so there is nothing to link the asker to, and the answer has to be written by someone who saw the failure.

- #3652 — [Question] Which documented macOS API, if any, can move a window belonging to another appli
- #3653 — [Question] What primary evidence establishes version compatibility for SIP-enabled native m
- #3663 — [Question] For a macOS Accessibility window mover, how should bounded size-position-size op

_Shared vocabulary that grouped them: `macos`, `window`._

## Deliverable

**An answer, posted as a comment on each question issue above.** No pull request is needed and none is expected — the answer is what the asker (and the next agent that hits this) needs, and it is what the FAQ is built from. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies an `answered` comment into D1, and from then on `misakanet_search` returns it as a `type: faq` hit.

The answer has to be *observed*, not generated. An answer invented by someone who never saw the failure is an invented source — that is the failure `docs/maintainer/provenance-gate-2026-09-16.md` exists to prevent. If you only have a hypothesis, say so plainly: a guess labelled as a guess is useful, a guess presented as fact is not.

leads.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
leads.description: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject

leads.title: Show HN: JavaScript web apps with WASM layout and GPU rendering in 280 KB
leads.description: Over the past year, I have been working to find a better way to write cross-platform apps. The problems I am trying to solve: - Native frameworks only work on a subset of platforms, so a different implementation of the UI needs to be written per target. - They are updated at the same pace as the platform itself, which forces the developer to split the user base to be able to use new features, or wait a long time for bugs to get fixed. - They also force developers to use specific high-level languages, so they are not a good fit for apps with high performance requirements, like creative apps or games. - Cross-platform frameworks that rely on bundling a browser engine solve the problem of code reuse, but they inherit the limitations of HTML/CSS. - Those that take control over layout and rendering are not efficient and lightweight enough to be used on the web, and require the use of compiled languages. Ideally, we would be able to bundle the UI framework directly with the application. This would allow developers to use new features and fix issues in the UI framework immediately. It would also allow ideas for improvements to compete in a natural way, rather than being decided by a committee. Uniform is my idea for how we can solve these problems. This is the structure: - A layout and rendering engine written in C, compiled to WASM on the web and native code on all other platforms - A JavaScript API where each function call gets forwarded directly into the core, for best performance and efficiency - A native runtime (<2 MB) that makes it possible to run the same JavaScript code on macOS and iOS (more platforms to come). The runtime can also generate packaged apps to upload to app stores. The packaging steps are also described in JS. Uniform supports very fast iteration cycles via hot-reload on all platforms. Even on iOS, the JS source code of an app can be changed while the app is running. Changes are visible on the next display refresh. No connection to a computer or the internet is required. Apps can be written from scratch on a phone, with native performance. The readme in the linked repository includes many examples and a detailed explanation of the core ideas. It is handwritten without any use of AI. And here is a live demo: https://raffk.com/hn-demo/ It should work in any browser that supports WebGPU. (To get 120 Hz support in Safari, the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” feature flag needs to be disabled.)

leads.title: This Industrial Revolution Belongs to the Builders
leads.description: You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0. Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead. They're wrong. Because as a builder/founder, you create value. Capital must capture some of this value to have a return. The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead). So this means that Capital ~= Labor. But that's a problem for the "owners of capital will own everything" narrative, because now we have: AI = Labor = Capital -> 0 In practice this will happen slowly as builders need less and less capital to build, capital will increasingly struggle to capture value created by builders. Counterintuitively this means valuations will climb dramatically reflecting capital paying more and more to capture less and less value from builders. As disruption accelerates, volatility increases while broader market wide returns start to stagnate. The net will be a wholesale wealth and power transfer from capital holders to builders/founders, on the magnitude of what happened between the aristocracy and the capitalist class in the earlier industrial revolutions. It's already started, companies are raising later and at higher valuations. Most people accept that if superintelligence were created, capital would be useless, but what they often don't realize is that a class of builders armed with AI is already creating a distributed superintelligence that will have the same effect. Interested if anyone else shares this perspective.
