leads.title: Show HN: Zigzag, a native Mac browser for people leaving Arc
leads.description: Hello HN! I am Zigao, a high school student from Shanghai. I am new to HN so hello to y’all! I used Arc everyday, and I never had any issues with it. So when The Browser Company announced that they will shut down Arc on Dec 22 I was devastated. I don’t want to switch back to boring tabs along the top. Everything else i’ve tried is either a Chromium fork or an AI integrated browser that I don’t want. Therefore, I’ve been building my own browser for the last three weeks. Its name is Zigzag, a free and open source Mac browser that works just like Arc, written in Swift and based on WebKit. It is lightweight and fast. Zigzag has: - The stuff you missed from Arc (obviously, that’s the point)... - Import from Arc (or any other browser) brings everything (your spaces, pins, history, passwords, cookies, etc) - Chrome extension support! Even though its based on WebKit, you can install them from the Chrome Web Store. Extensions such as 1Password, Bitwarden, dark reader, Return Youtube Dislike, Tampermonkey all work) And most importantly: - Privacy: no account, no telemetry, no analytics - Free and open source: no one can shut it down, anyone can contribute and fork their own copy! - It’s tiny and fast! Around 18 MB installed (Arc is over 800 MB), no Chromium, no Electron (eww) Some minor features that are nice-to-haves: - Built in ad blocker using uBlock origin’s and Easylist’s filter lists - Cookie popups turned down for you automatically, never accepted - Split view up to four pages, drag pages intuitively - Install any website as apps (still polishing it) - Developer mode for web devs - Little Arc (called Zigzag Mini) - AI apps can use your browser if you want (MCP, off by default), stop button built in - AppleScript and Shortcuts support, written in the conventional way Why WebKit? - I once tried to fork Helium and build on that. But the source was around 100 GB and builds took 3 to 4 hours on my Mac. Shipping Chromium is nearly impossible for me as a solo dev - Battery and RAM: WebKit is built for Mac by Apple, its generally easier on battery and memory than Chromium - Native: Swift + WebKit = behaves like a real Mac app, explained later (e.g. Zen) - Chrome extensions already works on Zigzag, so the point of using Chromium is mostly gone Why not Zen or Orion? I tried both before building this, because I was looking for alternatives. They are good browsers, just not what I wanted. Zen is based on Firefox. It is basically an Arc replica but it’s a Firefox under the hood, so you get Firefox extensions instead of Chrome extensions, and it doesn’t really feel like a native Mac app, which was kinda backwards. If you love Firefox it’s great, but it didn’t feel like Arc to me. Orion is the closest to what I wanted in terms of speed, lightweightness and nativeness (are these even words?). It is WebKit and runs Chrome extensions. But it is closed sourced, and it is nowhere like Arc. It has vertical tabs but no real spaces, pins or favorites like Arc. It feels like a Safari clone instead of an Arc clone, so I turned it down. I love how it supports Chrome extensions, so that’s why I’ve done the same in Zigzag. So how do Chrome extensions work on WebKit? This is probably the part people ask about the most, so here you go. In macOS 15.4, Apple added web extension support to WebKit itself. Safari only takes extensions that come wrapped in an app from the App store, but the engine underneath can load a normal Chrome extension folder. So when you click “Add to Zigzag” on the Chrome Web Store, Zigzag downloads the extension straight from Google. It checks its signatures, unpacks it, and hands it to WebKit. That’s the easy part, and frankly most WebKit browsers can do that easily. However, WebKit doesn’t have every Chrome API. Stuffy like history, bookmarks, downloads, side panels, notifications and a few others just aren’t there. So Zigzag fills those in itself. When an extension calls one, Zigzag answers it, but only if that extension asked for that

leads.title: [Bounty] Faster decode GEMVs for IQ1_S, IQ1_M and IQ2_*, bit for bit
leads.description:
> **Reserved:** this bounty is reserved for an invited contributor. Unsolicited claims and pull requests for it will be closed.

## Setup (once)

Written for an RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB, Blackwell sm_120); any NVIDIA GPU from sm_80 works. Linux, WSL2 or Windows (on
Windows, build from an "x64 Native Tools" prompt so nvcc finds MSVC). sm_120 needs the CUDA toolkit 12.8 or newer and a
torch built for CUDA 12.8 or newer.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crit-labs/crit.git
cd crit
git checkout -b iq-gemv-speed
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate              # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install ninja pytest numpy gguf
pip install -e core/python -e .
nvcc --version                         # must be on PATH
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,compute_cap --format=csv
# builds for this GPU (cached in ~/.cache/crit/kernels), then the tests must pass before you change anything
crit kernels build gguf-rows
python -m pytest kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/tests -q
```

Read before you start: `docs/CONTRIBUTION_CRITERIA.md`, `kernels/TEMPLATES.md`, `kernels/core/README.md` and
`kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/README.md`.

## Task

gguf-rows' decode GEMV (structure `gemv`, 1 to 8 rows) reads the 4- to 8-bit GGUF formats at 71-96% of an RTX 5090's
copy bandwidth, but the 1- and 2-bit IQ formats only at 50-65%: IQ1_S 732-771 GB/s, IQ1_M 754-796, IQ2_XXS 930-948,
IQ2_XS 942-998, IQ2_S 953-1,018 (1 row on 14336 x 4096 and 4096 x 14336, weights read cold; the 5090 copies at
1,487 GB/s). At 1.6 to 2.6 bits a weight the decode, not the memory read, sets the time: IQ1_S's 11.5 MB matrix takes
15 us against 7.7 us of reading. Each lane decodes one 32-value sub-block at a time through four dependent grid lookups,
the grids in global memory (L1-cached).

Make the five formats' gemv faster without changing a single output bit.

## Levers to try

- Two or more sub-blocks a lane in flight, so one sub-block's grid lookups overlap another's dot products. The order in
  which a lane adds its terms must stay the same (see "The declared order", step 3): decode ahead, add in order.
- The grids (up to 16 KB for IQ1_S) staged into shared memory once a block.
- Each lever as a knob of the `gemv` structure in `kernel.json` (with the old behaviour as one of its values) so the
  sweep picks it per format, shape and GPU. The current WARPS / SPLITS defaults were chosen on Q4_K, Q6_K and Q8_0.

The code: `kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/gguf_rows_cuda/gguf_rows.cu` (the gemv kernel), the IQ decoders in
`kernels/core/include/crit_kcore/gguf.cuh` and the grids in `gguf_grids.cuh`. Knobs in code: `kernels/TEMPLATES.md`,
"Knobs in code".

## Exactness gates

The declared order does not change, so the existing tests pass unchanged, for every format (not only the five):

- `test_gemv_is_the_declared_order_bit_for_bit_and_a_rows_bits_its_own`, `test_every_split_is_its_own_declared_order`,
  `test_a_gathered_row_equals_the_plain_call_on_its_expert`, `test_a_nan_reaches_its_rows_outputs_and_no_others`,
  `test_the_device_iq_grids_are_cores` (a grid copied into shared memory must still come from the same table).
- `crit kernels sweep` checks every knob configuration against the declared order bit for bit: no mismatch.
- `crit kernels gates` passes (nonfinite, repeat, edges, sums, register and shared-memory limits for every
  architecture in kernel.json).

## Done-check

Save as `iq.json`:

```json
{"gemv": [{"format": "IQ1_S", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "IQ1_S", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}, {"format": "IQ1_M", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "IQ1_M", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}, {"format": "IQ2_XXS", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "IQ2_XXS", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}, {"format": "IQ2_XS", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "IQ2_XS", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}, {"format": "IQ2_S", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "IQ2_S", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}]}
```

Before changing anything (right after the setup), measure today's kernel:

```sh
crit kernels sweep gguf-rows --shapes iq.json --out before
```

When your change is done, with nothing else running on the GPU:

```sh
python -m pytest kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/tests -q
crit kernels gates gguf-rows --shapes iq.json
crit kernels sweep gguf-rows --shapes iq.json --out after
```

Compare the best 1-row time for each of the 10 shapes in `before` and `after` (the sweep's report). On the reference
RTX 5090 every shape must be at least 20% faster after, and no other format slower (a maintainer also runs the sweep on
Q4_K, Q6_K and Q8_0 shapes). The 5060 Ti's numbers go in the pull request as well: its gain may differ, since it has
less bandwidth for the same decode work.

## Rules

- Comment on this issue before you start, so nobody else works on it at the same time.
- Every constant that only changes speed (warps, tiles, splits, values in flight) is a knob in the kernel's
  `kernel.json` with a default, tuned by `crit kernels sweep`, never a number picked on one GPU.
- Do not loosen any existing test, tolerance or check. The tests this issue says to change are the only ones to change.
- Keep the kernel's declared order (its README's "Numerics" and "declared order") unless this issue says otherwise.
- Update the kernel's README (applicability, numerics, measured speed with the GPU named), and add a line under the top
  section of `CHANGELOG.md`.
- One focused pull request from your fork into `main`, its description starting with `Closes #<this issue>`.

## Submit

In the pull request description paste: your GPU line from `nvidia-smi` above, the full output of every command under
"Done-check", and the before and after times of every shape from the two sweep reports.

A maintainer runs the same commands on the reference RTX 5090. The bounty is paid when they pass there as well and the

leads.title: [Bounty] gguf-rows reads the ternary TQ1_0 and TQ2_0 formats
leads.description:
> **Reserved:** this bounty is reserved for an invited contributor. Unsolicited claims and pull requests for it will be closed.

## Setup (once)

Written for an RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB, Blackwell sm_120); any NVIDIA GPU from sm_80 works. Linux, WSL2 or Windows (on
Windows, build from an "x64 Native Tools" prompt so nvcc finds MSVC). sm_120 needs the CUDA toolkit 12.8 or newer and a
torch built for CUDA 12.8 or newer.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crit-labs/crit.git
cd crit
git checkout -b gguf-ternary
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate              # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install ninja pytest numpy gguf
pip install -e core/python -e .
nvcc --version                         # must be on PATH
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,compute_cap --format=csv
# builds for this GPU (cached in ~/.cache/crit/kernels), then the tests must pass before you change anything
crit kernels build gguf-rows
python -m pytest kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/tests -q
```

Read before you start: `docs/CONTRIBUTION_CRITERIA.md`, `kernels/TEMPLATES.md`, `kernels/core/README.md` and
`kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/README.md`.

## Task

gguf-rows multiplies activation rows by a matrix kept in its stored GGUF block format. It reads 20 formats but not the
two ternary ones, TQ1_0 (type id 34) and TQ2_0 (type id 35). Add both, to every call: `gemv` (1 to 8 rows, plain and
gathered over experts), `gemm` (any rows, s8 tensor cores) and `dequantize`, and let the gguf-projections plugin take
them.

## The formats

The authoritative definition is gguf-py's decoder, `gguf/quants.py`, classes `TQ1_0` and `TQ2_0` (installed above as
`gguf`; read it with `python -c "import gguf.quants, inspect; print(inspect.getsource(gguf.quants.TQ1_0))"`). In short,
both have 256 values a block and one FP16 scale `d`, each value `(code - 1) * d` with codes 0, 1 or 2:

- TQ2_0, 66 bytes: 64 bytes of 2-bit codes, four a byte, then `d`.
- TQ1_0, 54 bytes: 48 bytes of five base-3 codes a byte, 4 bytes of four base-3 codes a byte, then `d`. The codes come
  out of a byte by gguf-py's multiply-by-a-power-of-3-and-shift rule; follow it exactly.

Both fit gguf-rows' declared order as formats with one scale a 32-value sub-block (`s = d`, the integer codes
`code - 1`), so no new kind of term is needed: see the README's "The declared order", step 2.

## Where the code goes

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `core/python/crit_core/model/gguf_blocks.py` | `TYPES`, `BLOCKS`, `SCALE_BYTES` entries and the host decoders behind `subblocks()` and `stored_values()` for 34 and 35. The tests and `bench.py`'s reference `product()` use these, so they must equal gguf-py bit for bit |
| `kernels/core/include/crit_kcore/gguf.cuh` | the device decoders (the type enum, block bytes, the decode of a sub-block into int8 codes and its FP32 scale), beside the existing formats' |
| `kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/gguf_rows_cuda/gguf_rows.cu` and `gguf_rows.h` | accept the two types wherever the formats are dispatched |
| `kernels/techniques/projections/gguf-rows/tests/test_gguf_rows.py` | the format-parametrized tests pick the new formats up from `BLOCKS` on their own. `test_what_the_kernel_cannot_read_is_refused` uses type 34 as its unreadable example: switch it to a type gguf-rows still does not read (for example 1, F16) |
| `inference/gguf-projections/entry.json` | drop the ternary formats from `avoid_when` |
| `inference/gguf-projections/tests/test_plugin.py` | line ~156 uses `gguf:TQ1_0` as a refused type: switch it to one still refused, and add a TQ2_0 matrix to a test that loads and runs the plugin |
| `kernels/crit_kernels/tests/test_sweep.py` | line ~125 lists a TQ2_0 tensor the sweep skips: it should now be listed as a matrix |
| READMEs | gguf-rows' Applicability table, `core/python/crit_core/model/README.md` (~line 225), the comment at the top of `gguf.cuh` |

## Exactness gates

All of these pass with TQ1_0 and TQ2_0 among the parametrized formats:

- `test_stored_values_equal_the_formats_reference_decoder`: host decoder, FP32 `dequantize` and BF16 `dequantize`
  against gguf-py's `dequantize`, bit for bit.
- `test_gemv_is_the_declared_order_bit_for_bit_and_a_rows_bits_its_own`: gemv against the declared order at 1, 2, 3,
  5 and 8 rows, in BF16, FP16 and FP32.
- `test_every_split_is_its_own_declared_order`, `test_a_gathered_row_equals_the_plain_call_on_its_expert`,
  `test_a_nan_reaches_its_rows_outputs_and_no_others`.
- `test_the_prompt_gemm_is_gemvs_order_bit_for_bit`, `test_the_prompt_gemm_staged_in_chunks_has_the_same_bits`.
- Every other test in the three test files named above, unchanged.

          {"format": "TQ2_0", "N": 14336, "K": 4096}, {"format": "TQ2_0", "N": 4096, "K": 14336}],

leads.title: Show HN: A booking page that handles payment and sends a Zoom/Meet/Discord link
leads.description: Programming used to be the fun part. Sit with a problem for a week, get it working at night, the thing is yours. The idea of bootstrapping your SaaS and breaking out in the industry used to be exciting, but now everything is a prompt and can be built by anyone, in a weekend. What nobody wants to do is keep it running and maintain it. I think big SaaS will survive, but a small SaaS business is hard to sell. I know building is cheap, maintaining is the actual work, and the part I decided to take on. Since the end of July I have been building this alone. Consultants, Coaches, tutors, I know are selling sessions with linktree + calendly + stripe link or "dm me on discord", and also struggle using discord as the place to host the session, like Google Meet or Zoom. Which means making a voice channel by hand for every call. Now it's one page: people pick a time, pay if it's a paid session, and the call link is made for them on discord, zoom or google, sent in the email. I built a discord bot that turns discord into a meeting platform like Zoom or Google Meet. Add the bot to your server, run /setup, members can book with /book on the server or from the page, and 15 min before the start it makes a voice channel where only the creator and the booker can see. One thing I'm not sure about: no fixed price. A booking is a request with an offer starting from the base price, the creator accepts or declines. Clever or annoying, you tell me. Take a look at mine https://shinetr.ee/poty or type /book in https://discord.gg/SfEVf2yFPT . The dashboard lets you fully customize how you would like. I don't know if this takes off. Trying to get users right now and their feedback. But the few months of building it were the first time in a while that I closed the laptop and felt like I made something, and I wanted to put it in front of people who would get that especially with all the fear mongering of software development is over. If you sell sessions, or you want to build something like this together, write me. I will be in the comments all day.

leads.title: Show HN: Rebuilding Amazon SES in Rust
leads.description: I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend. Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control. We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine. We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider. Keep the SES integration For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration: import boto3 ses = boto3.client( "sesv2", region_name="us-east-1", endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com", ) For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/ Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery. Engine Messages per second NitroMTA 3,313 KumoMTA 1,048 Postfix with OpenDKIM 806 Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it. The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid. KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately. The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/ Give each IP a budget for each provider An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off. We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it. With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung. The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable. Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records. Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

leads.title: Platform-Capitalism on Steroids
leads.description: So i got recently unemployed, left my last company as they wanted me to leave. They offered me money to leave and as they changed my working environment in an unpleasant way I decided to take the money. So now i find myself on the job market for IT specialists right in the middle of AI take-over. The jobs are shifting towards AI automation or so. At least any code seems to be written now by AI, and in the best case reviewed by a human. After thinking for a few days what job i am interested in, talking about it to AI, i start feeling over-helmed by the requirements companies are asking for. Are there already Senior AI Architects in Germany? Not sure. Anyway, how do these changes concern me? Looking at the job market, everything is nowadays Frontend, DevOps, Finance or Embedded it seems. Common Software Development vanished except for a few jobs at old-fashioned companies. I wonder who is developing all those tools and libraries? This are spare time projects multi-trillion-dollar companies are built on. Finally all application code is written either for iOS, Android or Web. Which eventually maps to Swift, Kotlin and html5/css/Javascript. And Embedded is another field, hardware product development. Which I am just not motivated anymore. So where to go from here now? What are the options? Finally dealing more with people, dealing more with what? Where to head from here? Damn i lost traction in the market. Now spinning around myself. What is truly needed? Can this even be determined as the market is changing so quickly? One things is definitely important. Build systems which not only build but track, verify and release changes while still allowing quick rollbacks. Right? People want to deploy very quickly new features to their customers while letting the customer test, but bugs are still possible, so rollbacks will be more important than ever. Will they? The tricky will still be, while people using this new infrastructure, they feed AI with the solution training it themselves to replace their works putting them into a situation where they need to try stay ahead of the machine's skills. The faster they hustle the more they improve the machine, which does not need to breath. The better the machine the more you hustle. It/IT looks to me like a mouse in a spinning wheel. Platform-Capitalism on Steroids.

leads.title: Show HN: VoxaDub – Open-source AI video dubbing with speaker-aware voices
leads.description: Hi HN, I have been working on a project called VoxaDub: an open source local-first AI dubbing tool which can translate videos into other languages while preserving the original voices of the speakers. A major issue when translating is ensuring the translation matches with the length of speech in the target language. Even slight differences in timing can cause unnatural dubbing. It becomes more complex when there are multiple speakers in the original video. I have created a pipeline that uses Whisper/WhisperX to transcribe and align audio, Community-1 to identify speakers, Hy-MT2 to translate contextually and VoxCPM2 to generate speaker aware audio. The main feature of VoxaDub is the ability to improve the translation using the available time for the audio to be spoken for, limit the time changes to within certain bounds and analyse for any timing issues. There is also some experimental Live Dubbing for YouTube videos and live streams through a Chrome extension. This is actively being developed and is not yet production ready. The main project runs fully locally once models are set up, no external translation or TTS APIs are required. Optional GPU usage is available using Colab and Modal. I am pleased to see that the project was recently added to the Ecosystem & Community section of OpenBMB's official VoxCPM GitHub repository (PR #389). While this is just a community project listing it was nice to see this progress. True examples of the English to Spanish, Japanese and Turkish dubbing can be found in the README. Source videos, information on how it was implemented and any limitations are also present. The project is MIT licensed and can be found on GitHub. I would really appreciate any technical feedback on the timing of the translations, speaker consistency and simplifying the local setup. There is a lot of room for improvement so any thoughts would be great!

leads.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
leads.description: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.
